clean_body: I'm proud to stand with Darline Graham, and I'm asking you to do the same. | Peter, Darline Graham is a principled conservative leader and a strong advocate for South Carolina families. And I am proud to give her my full support. Darline’s brother and my dear friend, Lindsey Graham, served South Carolina with distinction. Darline carries that same sense of duty into this fight in her own way. Peter, she is not a career politician. She spent nearly thirty years serving South Carolina before she ever ran for anything, and she stepped into this race the same way she has approached everything else in her life: because it was needed, not because she wanted the title. Her Democrat opponent, with the help of the National Democrats, has raised nearly $11 million to try to flip this seat. Hollywood donors and DC insiders think that if they can pour enough money into this race, they can elect the most radical Democrat ever nominated for statewide office in South Carolina. Every attack ad between now and November is designed to convince South Carolina that her Democrat opponent isn’t a radical, paid gun control advocate or a leader of “White Women for Kamala Harris.” Darline’s Democrat opponent opposed South Carolina's law keeping girls' sports for girls. If she’s elected, she’ll back expanding the U.S. Supreme Court. We know better, but right now, Darline doesn’t have the same resources to set the record straight. Darline has already proved she can lead in just a few short months in the Senate, and I know she will continue representing South Carolina with the same purpose and commitment her brother did. South Carolina deserves a senator who has already spent a lifetime proving she will fight for it. Thank you, Tom Cotton | | Paid for by Darline Graham Majority Fund, a joint fundraising committee authorized by and composed of Darline for Senate, Fund for America's Future, Security is Strength PAC, and NRSC. 228 S. | | | Yesterday, the Supreme Court ruled in our favor on mail-in voting.That should be the end of the story. It's not.For weeks, the Trump administration threw every legal challenge it could at vote-by-mail — and lost, again and again. As I told the _New York Times_ after the ruling: the real question is how many times does this president have to lose before he gets the hint. **States run our elections, not Presidents. **
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139255002/646761164/-569431239?refcode=260915-notenough&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDcvMS83NzI2MCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIxZTZlMGQ1NS0yZmIxLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=Ab_9EaZBm0hwFhl2bjVUNgrSt6XylVrZ9FSkGLqlzho=)
---
But here's the problem. Winning in court doesn't undo the damage those challenges already did. The two most important factors in any campaign are money and time.
#
Peter,
At this point in the election, every organization starts making tough decisions. VoteVets is no different in that regard, and we need to tell you about the call we just made.
The two most important factors in any campaign are money and time. With less than 50 days until the election, time is running out. And with millions of dollars in spend across dozens of states and races behind us, the tank is running low. Real low.
VoteVets candidates will win majorities in the House and Senate if we have the resources we need to support them. But the difficult truth today is that our fundraising has slowed down, and that’s left us with decisions to make.
We can pull back and lower our budgets to be more in line with our fundraising, knowing we might lose races we could otherwise win. Or, we stay the course on our current budget, even though we know that risks leaving us in the red after Election Day.
Do you know the motto of the British Special Air Service, Peter? **“Who dares wins.”** VoteVets didn’t get this far without taking risks. We decided to stay the course.
We did it because this election is too important. But we also did it because we’ve got a team of committed supporters behind us, Peter. People like you. And today, we’re counting on you to help us raise what we need to close this budget gap.

# Terms of Service
Community stewardship in the data center era, now on demand
Thank you for joining Americans for Responsible Innovation for a conversation about what communities can ask for when a data center comes to town. Four officials from four states, elected under different party labels and working in very different institutions, walked through how these agreements are actually being negotiated, what residents have managed to secure on energy, water, and tax terms, and where the process still closes before the public gets a look at the deal.

**The full recording is below, and it is public.** If someone in your network is watching a project move through their own community, this is a useful hour to send them.

# Peter,
---
There's now a law in California with my name associated with it. Everyone in Sacramento knows exactly what the **"Stop Nick Shirley Act"** means. On August 22nd, Governor Newsom signed AB 2624. Three days later, I was standing at the State Capitol with a crowd of people who showed up because they understood what this law _actually_ does.

Supporters say it protects immigration workers from harassment. Here's what it really does, Peter: **it makes it harder for anyone -- me included -- to investigate where your tax dollars are being sent.** I said it plainly at the rally: this is not the end; _this is just the beginning._ Because here's the part that should bother you more than anything else. **The assemblymember who wrote this bill is married to California's Attorney General** -- the _one person_ in this state whose entire job is supposed to be going after fraud. Instead, his wife wrote the bill that makes it harder to expose it. That's not a coincidence, Peter. I've spent the last year showing up where legacy media won't -- daycare centers, tax-funded nonprofits, the offices of people who'd rather I disappear than answer a question. That work is exactly why a state legislature decided to write a law with my name on it instead of going after the fraud I keep finding. A state senator at the rally called it unconstitutional. A city attorney called it a direct threat to the First Amendment. _They're right_ -- and they're not going to be the ones who stop it. It's Elaine Luria, and Raja said I could reach out.

On November 8th, 2022, after a difficult, expensive, and hard-fought reelection campaign, I called my opponent to offer my concession and congratulations.
It wasn't a pleasant call to make. But I've never second-guessed the decisions that led me there.
If we haven't met: I entered the Naval Academy at 17 and spent 20 years in the Navy as a nuclear engineer, my entire career aboard combatant ships.
In 2018, I ran for Congress and flipped Virginia's 2nd District.
I'm also a mom, which is still the best job I've ever had.
In Congress, I served on the January 6th Committee, knowing full well it could cost me my seat. That cycle, outside far-right groups spent $6,059,677 against me. Add a national environment that was brutal for frontline Democrats, and I came up short.
_**For me, the worst outcome isn’t losing a fight. It’s going down with no fight at all.**_
So I'm back, running to win this seat back from Jen Kiggans, because I can't sit on the sidelines and watch our country descend into chaos.
The Cook Political Report rates VA-02 a Toss-Up. This is one of Democrats’ best pickup opportunities in the country.

Team: The Supreme Court dropped another "shadow docket" ruling last night, finally blocking**Trump and the USPS from implementing his anti-mail-in voting Executive Order**. For the midterms, at least.Again, if this is new for you: **The "_shadow docket_."** It's the Supreme Court's way to review cases quickly without formal hearings. It's a construct of the last few decades, not widely used before then, but tons of unsigned, pro-Trump rulings have been issued from the Supreme Court this way the last few years. This was another ruling offered on _procedural grounds_ and not the merits of the law. **The 7-2 decision will stop the Department of Homeland Security and the Postal Service from creating a national voter registration list** and usurping the constitutional authority of the states to run our elections. clean_body: Mail-in ballots seem safe from Trump's USPS order for 2026, at least| | | | | | | | | = Team: The Supreme Court dropped another "shadow docket" ruling last night, finally blockingTrump and the USPS from implementing his anti-mail-in voting Executive Order. For the midterms, at least.Again, if this is new for you: The "shadow docket." It's the Supreme Court's way to review cases quickly without formal hearings. It's a construct of the last few decades, not widely used before then, but tons of unsigned, pro-Trump rulings have been issued from the Supreme Court this way the last few years. This was another ruling offered on procedural grounds and not the merits of the law. The 7-2 decision will stop the Department of Homeland Security and the Postal Service from creating a national voter registration list and usurping the constitutional authority of the states to run our elections. Even after Justice Kavanaugh signaled that he would have ruled in favor of Trump on the merits of the case, just that it was too close to the midterms for him to support the case right now, a 6-3 win is still worth celebrating in the current political environment, where opponents of voting rights control the White House, Congress, and the Supreme Court. This fight isn't over. The vote suppressors will take every inch they can in their battle to limit voting and invalidate your ballot. The harder they make it to vote, the more cynical, partisan politicians make voter participation feel worthless, the less people actually take part. = | | | = | | = | | | = | | = | | | = | | = | | | Experts and our compatriots in the pro-democracy movement were uncertain how the Supreme Court would handle this case. The Court’s past support of even the most legally dubious of Trump’s policies cast into doubt whether the justices would stand against his efforts here , especially after the Court rejected an earlier iteration of this challenge, just weeks ago , on the grounds that it was premature. “ The Supreme Court has made law totally unpredictable ,” election-law expert Justin Levitt told The Atlantic recently, while everyone waited for the Supreme Court to rule. He said “i n a normal world, there would be a zero percent chance ” that the Court would allow the USPS rule to go into effect. Yet, he went on, “ we don’t live in a normal world anymore.” For the time being, let’s celebrate that a semi-rational center of the court held, even as dangers remain ahead in both 2026 and 2028.Let's not forget, while we waited for the Supreme Court to rule, USPS rejected Leon County, Florida’s ballot design because its required printed notation about return mail was 0.014 of an inch too close to other information on the envelope. Trump, MAGA, and the vote suppressors aren't going to stop. He takes these legal decisions on the chin, then comes back with another Executive Order a short time later. He's going to work hard to mess with everyone's votes through this November and beyond. = | | | | | | | ---|---|---|--- Integrity First Voter Action Project is dedicated to expanding ballot access and increasing voter participation across the country. Since the Supreme Court gutted key provisions in the Voting Rights Act, extreme politicians have taken advantage to pass harsh laws that restrict access to the ballot box. These restrictions particularly affect disadvantaged communities and people of color. It’s our goal to bring awareness to these laws wherever they may crop up and organize voters to take action to ensure the right to vote is available to everyone in their states and communities. = = Contributions or gifts to Integrity First Voter Action Project are not tax-deductible as charitable contributions or as business expenses under IRC Section 162(3). He taught me about integrity, hard work, and doing the right thing, even when it isn't easy.
Those values have stayed with me throughout my life and public service. They're also why I sponsored legislation here in Ohio to protect girls' sports and ensure our daughters have a fair opportunity to compete.
Unfortunately, Marcy Kaptur has taken a very different approach in Washington. She voted to allow biological men to compete against girls in sports.
After 43 years in Congress, Marcy Kaptur has moved far outside the values of Northwest Ohio families.
I believe parents deserve a voice. I believe our daughters deserve fairness. And I believe we need leaders who aren't afraid to stand up for common sense.

| | "Then will the eyes of the blind be opened and _the ears of the deaf unstopped_." —Isaiah 35:5
---

That prophecy from Isaiah is not for the future, it's for today. It's the same reason Jesus said "anyone who believes in me will do the same works I have done, and even greater works..." And it's what today's _#TestimonyTuesday_ is all about. At our recent revival in Seattle, the Holy Spirit moved, and a young woman's hearing was FULLY RESTORED. And the whole thing was captured on video. You have to see it to believe. **[[WATCH THE MIRACLE MOMENT]](https://links.seanfeuchtministries.com/s/c/baEnuom4xPva-B9FXFaBiyS5ks9rR6PyQ5KHIteVdRrAbxxRrhQyvZheWecKG_MVA3ZSIqY9XQjPO1e771igis67AbOpxGgOjIL2jgZRAYBrbELM-cwJLCSo51hC64JNsBTKVlyDiHv1caQ3l-z5DFlgReO-2bCcJwqC_VQsixmqmY2RBH5KFsHXMK0mKVDjVBxZtWQEmrwRr6VYTml6C2AUWiMoHkFy3Rh_o-CdknJBrCprdkeRoyjov-2uY5pfNHc86r41RCd1Cx_ttMnGKkLoZlqZOmJibNQBNHr2eSy7SNGGCaXez9uwO2Vocat8IjWlV1_K2wRkqtoyBpOoty4nMjdfJb5KEX3e7fP1V9yB_60afX3b3xCMhFSATK5dFtKL78v4mPLMRwB5nUqzVhUCGqanMeBqLkxNXAsqOTqyW8OwJvucFDKK5k9u1H21qw/-8BtiS_6jeCVDU-KqJp5Mnwokr5Qwikv/24)** These kinds of miracles are commonplace at Let Us Worship revivals. Why? Because hearts are hungry for all God has for them. When the Holy Spirit finds great desperation and great faith, miracles follow. I hope this video encourages you today and reminds you to always keep a posture of faith, no matter what you're going through.

Hi Derek, it’s Lorenza Ramirez, the DNC’s National Organizing Director. I wanted to reach out because _**today**_ is National Voter Registration Day.
In a minute, I’m going to ask you to [**make a $7 contribution**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em-dnc-september-2026-gfr?amount=7&refcode=em_20260915_9175_fr&refcode2=9175_22930333_vfCm1n&akid=9175%2E22930333%2EvfCm1n) to the DNC, but first let me explain why:
For the last decade, Republicans have been registering more new voters than Democrats. It’s a big part of why they were able to win the House, the Senate, and the presidency in 2024.
And that’s why we made the strategic decision to invest in launching the largest voter registration program in the HISTORY of the Democratic Party.
But with voter registration deadlines coming up fast, we can’t slow down for a single second. That’s why we’re marking **_National Voter Registration Day_** by launching a massive push to reach, register, organize, and turnout voters in every part of America. Democrats across the country will mobilize to host voter registration drives and build power in their communities.
**And Derek, if we’re successful, this might just help us flip Congress and maintain power for years.**
Critical races, from your local school board to the Senate, could be decided by just a handful of votes in November. Registering new Democrats to vote could _literally_ be the difference between winning and losing in the years to come.
[**That’s why I’m asking you to chip in $7 today.**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em-dnc-september-2026-gfr?amount=7&refcode=em_20260915_9175_fr&refcode2=9175_22930333_vfCm1n&akid=9175%2E22930333%2EvfCm1n)
$7 to register thousands of new Democratic voters in key battleground states like Arizona and Nevada.
$7 to help us make calls, knock doors, and send texts to ensure _every_ Democrat has a plan to vote.
$7 to support work like this year after year — so we can take back Congress this year and the White House in 2028.
[**So Derek, will you chip in $7 to help us continue reaching voters? We’ve only got 49 days left until Election Day. The last time Mike Rogers made a run for the Senate, his congressional record on opioids weighed him down. Although his Democratic opponent, Rep. Elissa Slotkin, mostly avoided the issue, surrogates like state Sen. Rosemary Bayer gave him no quarter, pounding the former Republican congressman and FBI agent. "Since 2021, one Michigander has died every four hours from opioid use, but in Congress, Mike Rogers was a leading advocate for increased access to opioids," Bayer told a[ local reporter](https://substack.com/redirect/f5832264-f60a-4856-af19-57039ddff579?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Now running for another open Senate seat, Rogers is again attempting to escape and rewrite his long and well-illuminated record on opioids. When the local news site Michigan Bridge asked the candidate if he "wished he had taken a different approach to the opioid issue while in Congress," Rogers deflected, saying, "I understand that question is couched in a way that makes it sound terrible. I just disagree with the premise of the question." Elsewhere he has sought to pre-empt discussion of his opioid record by[ decrying Democrats](https://substack.com/redirect/95b17a65-247a-4ec6-878d-56d62f237479?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) who are "spreading lies," and by retroactively distorting and shrinking his work on the issue beyond recognition. "I voted to allow Americans who are suffering from debilitating pain to have access to the treatment they need to live comfortably, while keeping safeguards that prevent overprescription and addiction," he said.
Rogers' current Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, has been more aggressive than Slotkin, but is proving sloppy in the execution. He has[ mischaracterized](https://substack.com/redirect/5369d92e-5660-465f-9faa-7697c8a4c6a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Rogers as a former registered "lobbyist" for pharma and has[ anachronistically described](https://substack.com/redirect/6b80f7ca-fdd0-42f3-8ab0-d5c5fa283632?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) his onetime signature bill, the Pain Care Policy Act, first introduced in 2003, as "the legislation that kicked off the opioid epidemic."
But El-Sayed's errors do not disturb the greater truth in the charges. It is a matter of record that Rogers spent most of his 12 years in Congress tied at the policy hip with opioid-producer front-groups dedicated to expanding "pain awareness" and "reducing barriers to pain care." During his first four terms representing Michigan's 8th District, Rogers staked his name to an industry wish-list to expand and loosen access to opioids. This advocacy was no one-off vote, but a strategic and persistent focus of his career, maintained throughout the prescription-opioid epidemic's years of galloping growth.
The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

## "The 5th Vital Sign"
In 2001, the year Rogers entered Congress,[ 611 Michiganders](https://substack.com/redirect/331a5248-774d-458e-95ae-4e5c3d5e4180?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and[ 5,528 Americans](https://substack.com/redirect/d1b36b10-a31b-462e-8ba0-561e8ea2913b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) died by opioid overdose. These numbers signaled the continuation of a steady rise in fatal overdoses since the late-90s, with the sharpest spikes occurring in [rural America](https://substack.com/redirect/12f63cbb-af09-4bda-9620-8c34d2ece7b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But even if one chose to downplay or ignore the troubling data, no public official could claim ignorance about a brewing national opioid crisis. During Rogers' second month in office, the New York Times published a[ bombshell report](https://substack.com/redirect/0fe09b6e-48c4-47dd-b469-ec65946a0124?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on why "harried police detectives in dozens of rural areas in Eastern states are combating what they say is a growing wave of drug abuse involving a potent painkiller." A few months after that, West Virginia's attorney general filed the first lawsuit against Purdue Pharma for its marketing of Oxycontin, which the Food and Drug Administration soon slapped with a "black box warning."
"In Michigan, we had a good sense that the dial was turning from heroin to overprescribed opioids by the early 2000s," said Jonathan Stoltman, director of the Opioid Policy Institute in Grand Rapids, Michigan. "There were already janky local clinics in operation, and people were going across the border to pill mills in places like Toledo, Ohio. There were any number of data points where you could see what was happening--including Eminem songs."
Yet in September 2003, with overdose deaths continuing to rise, Rogers[ held a press conference](https://substack.com/redirect/27a62797-5b1e-4216-82da-cf593844c7ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to announce his sole sponsorship of a bill called the National Pain Care Policy Act. His first signature piece of legislation, Rogers introduced the bill flanked by Dr. Dick Payne, director of the American Pain Society, an industry-funded group notorious for its 1996 advocacy of the concept of pain as the "the 5th Vital Sign," considered a landmark development in the opioid crisis. Payne praised Rogers' bill for tackling what he called "the leading health problem in America today." The language used by both men tracked closely to the sales, educational, and lobbying lines of the same opioid manufacturers that[ underwrote the American Pain Society](https://substack.com/redirect/5d9c370e-7bce-49fb-8fea-ae4580378480?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to the tune of $1 million in traceable funding during the[ early 2000s](https://substack.com/redirect/9f40416d-f2bd-4022-bb5d-73bfc857709c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Most of the group's operating budget came from Purdue Pharma, whose CEO Richard Sackler described in private correspondence his company's "[good relationship](https://substack.com/redirect/710db2fe-a466-4d09-9382-0ed59aa85b87?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)" with the Society. Purdue and other opioid-makers also funded the American Pain Foundation, another multi-million dollar front group that "piloted mobilization strategies" and contributed to "strategic planning" for Rogers' Pain Care Act, according to a [presentation](https://substack.com/redirect/4f10654f-401e-488d-a212-89665a23c684?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) given at Purdue Pharma's headquarters in September of 2004.
Rogers' bill arrived at a unique moment in the opioid crisis. Although the problem was spreading and garnering more urgent attention in the media, opioid producers and their sales teams were still living high on the hog and remained arrogant about their ability to keep the good times rolling. Industry executives, still years away from copping plea deals and signing billion-dollar settlements, believed they could keep expanding the opioids market while deflecting responsibility for the resulting public health emergency onto its victims. Rogers' proposed Pain Care Act embodied this audacity. Supported by a Pain Society-funded radio and TV campaign, it sought to use the full might of the U.S. health bureaucracy to strengthen the intellectual and policy foundations of opioid normalization, access, and use.
## Reducing Barriers
Reflecting the urgency of what it called the nation's "leading health problem," Rogers' bill gave the White House until June 2004 to convene a Conference on Pain Care, chaired by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in order to "increase the recognition of pain as a significant public health problem" and "identify barriers to appropriate pain care [and] establish an agenda for action in both the public and private sectors _that will reduce such barriers_." [Emphasis added.] The bill further called for a federally funded national awareness campaign to "educate consumers, patients, their families, and other caregivers [about] the right of patients to have their pain promptly assessed, appropriately treated, and regularly reassessed, and to have their treatment adjusted if needed."
To help the public overcome any possible reticence in claiming their "right" to pain treatment, the campaign was to stress "the adverse physical, psychological, and financial consequences that can result if pain is not appropriately diagnosed or treated."
Rogers' bill did not specify a slogan for this campaign, but "Got Oxy?" would have been a catchy option.
To efficiently "reduce barriers" to pain treatment, the Pain Care Act proposed the creation of a National Center for Pain and Palliative Care Research--on par with the National Cancer Institute--that would manage six regional pain research centers. The new institutions would oversee an ongoing research program whose orbit of influence would include "schools, colleges, and universities, including schools of medicine and osteopathy, schools of pharmacy and pharmacology, schools of nursing, schools of dentistry, schools of physical therapy, schools of occupational therapy, and schools of clinical psychology, comprehensive health care centers and systems, and specialized centers of pain research or treatment."
To get this infrastructure up and running, Rogers called for apportioning $40 million annually through 2007. Much of this money would be distributed as grants for professional school training programs focused on "applicable laws on controlled substances, including the degree to which misconceptions concerning such laws or the enforcement thereof may create barriers to patient access to appropriate and effective pain care."
The flowchart at the center of Rogers' bill was based on ideas that industry was at the same time promoting through its echo chamber of front groups and corrupt medical institutions and thought leaders. Expressed in a blizzard of proposals for restructuring the NIH, the thrust of the message was simple: medical guidelines were still too conservative in determining the conditions that merited prescription opioids. The Pain Care Act would rectify this by funding federal research centers to develop treatment options for "all types of pain and pain-related symptoms; and conditions for which no widely accepted treatment options are yet available."
Sometimes the bill spoke of new "conditions," and sometimes it spoke of new "populations," but they were basically interchangeable. "In designing the public awareness campaign," proposed Section V of the Pain Care Act, "the Secretary shall take into account the need to reach underserved populations who are disproportionately under-treated for pain," including the elderly (Medicare Advantage programs) and veterans (the VA system).
A lawsuit filed by the state of Oklahoma against Johnson & Johnson in 2019 would[ uncover documents](https://substack.com/redirect/1872e098-3ded-4328-8d41-3142d00c6f9e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) revealing that the industry did not depend on the passage of Rogers' bill to target these "underserved populations." An initiative organized by Janssen Pharmaceuticals, called the "Imagine the Possibilities Coalition," ran unbranded campaigns to increase opioid use among the same populations named in Rogers' bill, including[ veterans](https://substack.com/redirect/f127bbe3-8577-476d-819a-f3833e6fd3df?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg),[ children](https://substack.com/redirect/1872e098-3ded-4328-8d41-3142d00c6f9e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) (through targeting school nurses and sports coaches), and the[ elderly](https://substack.com/redirect/3af8e2ec-5707-4bad-bc12-a06a271951a2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Despite the industry-funded media campaign and the best expert testimony money could buy, the Pain Care Policy Act stalled in committee throughout 2004. But Rogers pushed on. He reintroduced the bill in 2005, as the number of Americans[ killed by opioids passed 16,000](https://substack.com/redirect/019b43fe-7a3b-44ff-a444-411380bf95ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).**** When the bill died a second time, Rogers and his industry allies decided to regroup and reload, if not rebrand, before they tried again.
## An Epidemic of Addiction
Before introducing his bill a third time, Rogers co-sponsored another called the [National All Schedules Prescription Electronic Reporting Act of 2005](https://substack.com/redirect/3dcbdce5-22b7-463c-9cc8-62d8b5f589d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). The law, signed by George W. Bush in August of 2005, established a national prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) with the goal of identifying and stopping sketchy and unnecessary prescriptions. But the bill ignored the drug companies, who were already responsible for tracking their shipments, and who knew better than anyone when and where overprescribing was occurring.
PDMPs are "patient surveillance tools above all," in the words of medical sociologist Elizabeth Chiarello, and serve to shift attention back to individuals, not the institutions that were driving the crisis in the 2000s. The companies understood this, and saved their lobbying fire[ to defeat every attempt](https://substack.com/redirect/cb941077-cf27-4ff8-8072-f763514e4113?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that decade to enforce production caps and restrictive prescribing guidelines.
"The PDMP law did not address the supply-side of the equation, and by supporting it Rogers was still running cover for big pharma," said Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. "The data base was used to kick people unceremoniously off opioids after they were addicted, with no plan or attempt to move them into treatment. A lot of people think this was a big driver of the transition to heroin and the second wave of the crisis."
To this day, Rogers points to his support for the PDMP Act as proof of his commitment to address the opioid addiction crisis. He has less to say about his other activities in the mid-2000s, such as his headlining the debut event of the Pain Care Forum, an industry front group hatched to rally support for the Pain Care Policy Act.
The Pain Care Forum announced itself to the world in a June 2006 briefing on Capitol Hill titled "The Epidemic of Pain in America." In a now-familiar combo, the group was the brainchild of Purdue Pharma's chief lobbyist in Washington, Burt Rosen, and deployed Rogers as its congressional face. Cosponsored by the American Pain Society, the Pain Care Forum was designed to build support for Rogers' bill and reframe the spiraling opioid crisis as a familiar story of bad apples and addicts, rather than an epic tale of corruption and moral rot implicating drug companies, the house of medicine, Congress, and regulatory agencies responsible for protecting the public. At the Rogers event, speakers informed Congress that the "appropriate use of opioid medications like oxycodone is safe and effective and unlikely to cause addiction in people who are under the care of a doctor and who have no history of substance abuse."
The Pain Care Forum would go on to spend $750 million amplifying this message and pushing for Rogers' bill. This money was dispersed along a number of fronts, writes Chris McGreal in "American Overdose," including "pushing policies, writing legislation, and funding elected officials in Washington, DC, and across the country to promote opioids and oppose curbs on prescribing." When the covers were peeled back, McGreal writes, the forum was revealed to be little more than "a web of interwoven corporate interests and specialists in their pay." Its donors were a murderer's row of opioid producers, Purdue, Endo, and Abbott--Purdue's main subcontractor in selling OxyContin.
With media support and coaching from multiple front groups, Rogers reintroduced the Pain Care Policy Act in 2007, only to see it die a third time. In 2009, he tried again with the co-sponsorship of California Democrat Lois Capps, a[ pharma favorite](https://substack.com/redirect/f5dec660-8873-4960-83e6-8801bdc506b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) who had[ received $87,750](https://substack.com/redirect/f33336b3-4e6d-44fe-a191-44abd20a7805?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from Pain Care Forum backers since 2006, and Utah's Orrin Hatch, who like Rogers had received at least $300,000 from drug makers during roughly the same period.
The law once again failed to clear the Senate, but its supporters saw opportunity in the impending passage of Obama's healthcare reforms. After nearly seven years of defeat, they succeeded in stuffing a fair amount of Rogers' bill into the Affordable Care Act of 2010.
The biggest elements involved the creation of two official committees: the Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee and a 18-member expert panel tasked with producing a study for the non-profit Institute of Medicine (IOM), which carried the imprimatur of the National Academies.
Because the drug makers had so thoroughly seeded the pain research ecosystem, both committees were staffed by influential figures drenched in industry largesse. The Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee featured at least five members with strong industry connections who would go on to[ oppose restrictions on opioid prescribing](https://substack.com/redirect/4f9bbd99-0a5e-4ab3-a386-7b36f8e69bad?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) as "ridiculous," "horrible," and "shortsighted." The IoM committee was also chock-o-block with recipients of heavy industry funding, including Richard Payne of the American Pain Society, and academic researcher Myra Christopher, whose chair was endowed with a $1.5 million grant from Purdue Pharma.
## The Opioid Lobby
The IoM released its report, "[Relieving Pain in America](https://substack.com/redirect/030e81d8-696a-4877-9b40-1440ce8593e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)," in 2011, the year fatal opioid overdoses surpassed 17,000 and Purdue Pharma's OxyContin revenues reached $3 billion.
The authors understood that it was no longer 2003, and the document contains an obligatory reference to the need to expand the menu of non-drug pain treatments. But the drug makers and their front groups embraced the study because it delivered a gilded, National Academies-blessed validation of a foundational industry estimate and talking point: that more than 100 million American adults lived with chronic pain, at an annual cost to the economy of $635 billion. According to McGreal, Purdue Pharma's $150,000 campaign promoting "Relieving Pain in America" focused on these numbers. The wider opioid lobby also "swung its spotlight onto the headline figure of 100 million people in pain, claiming that this was the 'real epidemic,' not addiction."
As summarized years later by the New York Times, the IoM's 100 million figure "proved to be highly inflated [but] gave drugmakers another talking point for aggressive sales campaigns, primed doctors to prescribe opioids at an accelerating rate and [influenced the Food and Drug Administration](https://substack.com/redirect/c54fa0cb-e5ec-45e9-8410-a45e99381236?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to approve at least one highly potent opioid."
Some critics said as much at the time of the report's release. Dr. Nathaniel Katz, a pain specialist who chaired various FDA advisory committees, blasted "Relieving Pain in America" as "a political statement" that translated "compassion for patients with pain...into a model for opiate prescribing." Even at this late hour, however, it promised industry yet another boost, so long as the government was still asleep at the wheel. The FDA commissioner at the time, Margaret Hamburg, touted the IoM study's numbers upon its release, only to be later[ named in a lawsuit](https://substack.com/redirect/4d64daed-5490-4bb6-a1bb-61c16d5c0e9e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) alleging she and her husband profited directly from her approval of new drugs, including opioids, through their joint portfolio of pharmaceutical stocks.
The IoM report demonstrated that the industry's investments--in politicians like Rogers, front groups like the Pain Society, and influential researchers and medical organizations like those represented on the new Pain commissions--could still pay dividends. But opioids were increasingly seen in exactly the light industry most feared: not as a criminal or legal issue, but[ as a full-blown public health crisis](https://substack.com/redirect/ae78ca10-4a69-456b-8ac8-6c3d66febce2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Following the release of the controversial report, Rogers may have felt that his job was done, or realized that being the face of Pharma's pain agenda was a bad thing for an ambitious politician to be. Whatever the cause, in 2011 he pivoted fully to national security and became chair of the House Committee on Intelligence, a post he would hold until 2015, when he left Congress to consult for tech and defense companies.
It was a well-timed parachute jump. Within months, the American Pain Foundation self-dissolved following the Senate Finance Committee's announcement that it was[ launching an investigation](https://substack.com/redirect/4c3ed8e8-b67e-48b7-809b-564bf572739a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) into industry influence on opioid advocacy groups. (The American Pain Society would shutter its doors four years later.) In 2012, as Rogers was forcefully turning the page on his congressional career, 52,000 Americans overdosed on opioids, including 2,000 Michiganders.
By the time Rogers announced his first Senate campaign in 2023, the groups he'd worked with so closely during the 2000s were gone, but not forgotten. Their names routinely appeared in the $50 billion raft of[ opioid lawsuits](https://substack.com/redirect/b2cea879-e4bf-42dc-bf76-6a051e4328c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) being settled across the country.
"Rogers spent years in Congress pushing a bill that was clearly about training professionals to pump out more opioids, and worked behind the scenes with the companies that contributed to the crisis to get it passed," says Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. "At the end of the day, he was either stupid, an industry stooge, or both."

Photo by Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images. The last time Mike Rogers made a run for the Senate, his congressional record on opioids weighed him down. Although his Democratic opponent, Rep. Elissa Slotkin, mostly avoided the issue, surrogates like state Sen. Rosemary Bayer gave him no quarter, pounding the former Republican congressman and FBI agent. "Since 2021, one Michigander has died every four hours from opioid use, but in Congress, Mike Rogers was a leading advocate for increased access to opioids," Bayer told a. Now running for another open Senate seat, Rogers is again attempting to escape and rewrite his long and well-illuminated record on opioids. When the local news site Michigan Bridge asked the candidate if he "wished he had taken a different approach to the opioid issue while in Congress," Rogers deflected, saying, "I understand that question is couched in a way that makes it sound terrible. I just disagree with the premise of the question." Elsewhere he has sought to pre-empt discussion of his opioid record by who are "spreading lies," and by retroactively distorting and shrinking his work on the issue beyond recognition. "I voted to allow Americans who are suffering from debilitating pain to have access to the treatment they need to live comfortably, while keeping safeguards that prevent overprescription and addiction," he said. Rogers' current Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, has been more aggressive than Slotkin, but is proving sloppy in the execution. He has Rogers as a former registered "lobbyist" for pharma and has his onetime signature bill, the Pain Care Policy Act, first introduced in 2003, as "the legislation that kicked off the opioid epidemic." But El-Sayed's errors do not disturb the greater truth in the charges. It is a matter of record that Rogers spent most of his 12 years in Congress tied at the policy hip with opioid-producer front-groups dedicated to expanding "pain awareness" and "reducing barriers to pain care." During his first four terms representing Michigan's 8th District, Rogers staked his name to an industry wish-list to expand and loosen access to opioids. This advocacy was no one-off vote, but a strategic and persistent focus of his career, maintained throughout the prescription-opioid epidemic's years of galloping growth. The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment. | | ---|---|--- OxyContin pills, prescription only pain medication. Photo by Lawrence K. Ho/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images. "The 5th Vital Sign" In 2001, the year Rogers entered Congress, and died by opioid overdose. These numbers signaled the continuation of a steady rise in fatal overdoses since the late-90s, with the sharpest spikes occurring in . But even if one chose to downplay or ignore the troubling data, no public official could claim ignorance about a brewing national opioid crisis. During Rogers' second month in office, the New York Times published a on why "harried police detectives in dozens of rural areas in Eastern states are combating what they say is a growing wave of drug abuse involving a potent painkiller." A few months after that, West Virginia's attorney general filed the first lawsuit against Purdue Pharma for its marketing of Oxycontin, which the Food and Drug Administration soon slapped with a "black box warning." "In Michigan, we had a good sense that the dial was turning from heroin to overprescribed opioids by the early 2000s," said Jonathan Stoltman, director of the Opioid Policy Institute in Grand Rapids, Michigan. "There were already janky local clinics in operation, and people were going across the border to pill mills in places like Toledo, Ohio. There were any number of data points where you could see what was happening--including Eminem songs." Yet in September 2003, with overdose deaths continuing to rise, Rogers to announce his sole sponsorship of a bill called the National Pain Care Policy Act. His first signature piece of legislation, Rogers introduced the bill flanked by Dr. Dick Payne, director of the American Pain Society, an industry-funded group notorious for its 1996 advocacy of the concept of pain as the "the 5th Vital Sign," considered a landmark development in the opioid crisis. Payne praised Rogers' bill for tackling what he called "the leading health problem in America today." The language used by both men tracked closely to the sales, educational, and lobbying lines of the same opioid manufacturers that to the tune of $1 million in traceable funding during the. Most of the group's operating budget came from Purdue Pharma, whose CEO Richard Sackler described in private correspondence his company's "" with the Society. Purdue and other opioid-makers also funded the American Pain Foundation, another multi-million dollar front group that "piloted mobilization strategies" and contributed to "strategic planning" for Rogers' Pain Care Act, according to a given at Purdue Pharma's headquarters in September of 2004. Rogers' bill arrived at a unique moment in the opioid crisis. Although the problem was spreading and garnering more urgent attention in the media, opioid producers and their sales teams were still living high on the hog and remained arrogant about their ability to keep the good times rolling. Industry executives, still years away from copping plea deals and signing billion-dollar settlements, believed they could keep expanding the opioids market while deflecting responsibility for the resulting public health emergency onto its victims. Rogers' proposed Pain Care Act embodied this audacity. Supported by a Pain Society-funded radio and TV campaign, it sought to use the full might of the U.S. health bureaucracy to strengthen the intellectual and policy foundations of opioid normalization, access, and use. Reducing Barriers Reflecting the urgency of what it called the nation's "leading health problem," Rogers' bill gave the White House until June 2004 to convene a Conference on Pain Care, chaired by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in order to "increase the recognition of pain as a significant public health problem" and "identify barriers to appropriate pain care [and] establish an agenda for action in both the public and private sectors that will reduce such barriers." [Emphasis added.] The bill further called for a federally funded national awareness campaign to "educate consumers, patients, their families, and other caregivers [about] the right of patients to have their pain promptly assessed, appropriately treated, and regularly reassessed, and to have their treatment adjusted if needed." To help the public overcome any possible reticence in claiming their "right" to pain treatment, the campaign was to stress "the adverse physical, psychological, and financial consequences that can result if pain is not appropriately diagnosed or treated." Rogers' bill did not specify a slogan for this campaign, but "Got Oxy?" would have been a catchy option. To efficiently "reduce barriers" to pain treatment, the Pain Care Act proposed the creation of a National Center for Pain and Palliative Care Research--on par with the National Cancer Institute--that would manage six regional pain research centers. The new institutions would oversee an ongoing research program whose orbit of influence would include "schools, colleges, and universities, including schools of medicine and osteopathy, schools of pharmacy and pharmacology, schools of nursing, schools of dentistry, schools of physical therapy, schools of occupational therapy, and schools of clinical psychology, comprehensive health care centers and systems, and specialized centers of pain research or treatment." To get this infrastructure up and running, Rogers called for apportioning $40 million annually through 2007. Much of this money would be distributed as grants for professional school training programs focused on "applicable laws on controlled substances, including the degree to which misconceptions concerning such laws or the enforcement thereof may create barriers to patient access to appropriate and effective pain care." The flowchart at the center of Rogers' bill was based on ideas that industry was at the same time promoting through its echo chamber of front groups and corrupt medical institutions and thought leaders. Expressed in a blizzard of proposals for restructuring the NIH, the thrust of the message was simple: medical guidelines were still too conservative in determining the conditions that merited prescription opioids. The Pain Care Act would rectify this by funding federal research centers to develop treatment options for "all types of pain and pain-related symptoms; and conditions for which no widely accepted treatment options are yet available." Sometimes the bill spoke of new "conditions," and sometimes it spoke of new "populations," but they were basically interchangeable. "In designing the public awareness campaign," proposed Section V of the Pain Care Act, "the Secretary shall take into account the need to reach underserved populations who are disproportionately under-treated for pain," including the elderly (Medicare Advantage programs) and veterans (the VA system). A lawsuit filed by the state of Oklahoma against Johnson & Johnson in 2019 would revealing that the industry did not depend on the passage of Rogers' bill to target these "underserved populations." An initiative organized by Janssen Pharmaceuticals, called the "Imagine the Possibilities Coalition," ran unbranded campaigns to increase opioid use among the same populations named in Rogers' bill, including (through targeting school nurses and sports coaches), and the. Despite the industry-funded media campaign and the best expert testimony money could buy, the Pain Care Policy Act stalled in committee throughout 2004. But Rogers pushed on. He reintroduced the bill in 2005, as the number of Americans.** When the bill died a second time, Rogers and his industry allies decided to regroup and reload, if not rebrand, before they tried again. An Epidemic of Addiction Before introducing his bill a third time, Rogers co-sponsored another called the . The law, signed by George W. Bush in August of 2005, established a national prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) with the goal of identifying and stopping sketchy and unnecessary prescriptions. But the bill ignored the drug companies, who were already responsible for tracking their shipments, and who knew better than anyone when and where overprescribing was occurring. PDMPs are "patient surveillance tools above all," in the words of medical sociologist Elizabeth Chiarello, and serve to shift attention back to individuals, not the institutions that were driving the crisis in the 2000s. The companies understood this, and saved their lobbying fire that decade to enforce production caps and restrictive prescribing guidelines. "The PDMP law did not address the supply-side of the equation, and by supporting it Rogers was still running cover for big pharma," said Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. "The data base was used to kick people unceremoniously off opioids after they were addicted, with no plan or attempt to move them into treatment. A lot of people think this was a big driver of the transition to heroin and the second wave of the crisis." To this day, Rogers points to his support for the PDMP Act as proof of his commitment to address the opioid addiction crisis. He has less to say about his other activities in the mid-2000s, such as his headlining the debut event of the Pain Care Forum, an industry front group hatched to rally support for the Pain Care Policy Act. The Pain Care Forum announced itself to the world in a June 2006 briefing on Capitol Hill titled "The Epidemic of Pain in America." In a now-familiar combo, the group was the brainchild of Purdue Pharma's chief lobbyist in Washington, Burt Rosen, and deployed Rogers as its congressional face. Cosponsored by the American Pain Society, the Pain Care Forum was designed to build support for Rogers' bill and reframe the spiraling opioid crisis as a familiar story of bad apples and addicts, rather than an epic tale of corruption and moral rot implicating drug companies, the house of medicine, Congress, and regulatory agencies responsible for protecting the public. At the Rogers event, speakers informed Congress that the "appropriate use of opioid medications like oxycodone is safe and effective and unlikely to cause addiction in people who are under the care of a doctor and who have no history of substance abuse." The Pain Care Forum would go on to spend $750 million amplifying this message and pushing for Rogers' bill. This money was dispersed along a number of fronts, writes Chris McGreal in "American Overdose," including "pushing policies, writing legislation, and funding elected officials in Washington, DC, and across the country to promote opioids and oppose curbs on prescribing." When the covers were peeled back, McGreal writes, the forum was revealed to be little more than "a web of interwoven corporate interests and specialists in their pay." Its donors were a murderer's row of opioid producers, Purdue, Endo, and Abbott--Purdue's main subcontractor in selling OxyContin. With media support and coaching from multiple front groups, Rogers reintroduced the Pain Care Policy Act in 2007, only to see it die a third time. In 2009, he tried again with the co-sponsorship of California Democrat Lois Capps, a who had from Pain Care Forum backers since 2006, and Utah's Orrin Hatch, who like Rogers had received at least $300,000 from drug makers during roughly the same period. The law once again failed to clear the Senate, but its supporters saw opportunity in the impending passage of Obama's healthcare reforms. After nearly seven years of defeat, they succeeded in stuffing a fair amount of Rogers' bill into the Affordable Care Act of 2010. The biggest elements involved the creation of two official committees: the Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee and a 18-member expert panel tasked with producing a study for the non-profit Institute of Medicine (IOM), which carried the imprimatur of the National Academies. Because the drug makers had so thoroughly seeded the pain research ecosystem, both committees were staffed by influential figures drenched in industry largesse. The Interagency Pain Research Coordinating Committee featured at least five members with strong industry connections who would go on to as "ridiculous," "horrible," and "shortsighted." The IoM committee was also chock-o-block with recipients of heavy industry funding, including Richard Payne of the American Pain Society, and academic researcher Myra Christopher, whose chair was endowed with a $1.5 million grant from Purdue Pharma. The Opioid Lobby The IoM released its report, "," in 2011, the year fatal opioid overdoses surpassed 17,000 and Purdue Pharma's OxyContin revenues reached $3 billion. The authors understood that it was no longer 2003, and the document contains an obligatory reference to the need to expand the menu of non-drug pain treatments. But the drug makers and their front groups embraced the study because it delivered a gilded, National Academies-blessed validation of a foundational industry estimate and talking point: that more than 100 million American adults lived with chronic pain, at an annual cost to the economy of $635 billion. According to McGreal, Purdue Pharma's $150,000 campaign promoting "Relieving Pain in America" focused on these numbers. The wider opioid lobby also "swung its spotlight onto the headline figure of 100 million people in pain, claiming that this was the 'real epidemic,' not addiction." As summarized years later by the New York Times, the IoM's 100 million figure "proved to be highly inflated [but] gave drugmakers another talking point for aggressive sales campaigns, primed doctors to prescribe opioids at an accelerating rate and to approve at least one highly potent opioid." Some critics said as much at the time of the report's release. Dr. Nathaniel Katz, a pain specialist who chaired various FDA advisory committees, blasted "Relieving Pain in America" as "a political statement" that translated "compassion for patients with pain...into a model for opiate prescribing." Even at this late hour, however, it promised industry yet another boost, so long as the government was still asleep at the wheel. The FDA commissioner at the time, Margaret Hamburg, touted the IoM study's numbers upon its release, only to be later alleging she and her husband profited directly from her approval of new drugs, including opioids, through their joint portfolio of pharmaceutical stocks. The IoM report demonstrated that the industry's investments--in politicians like Rogers, front groups like the Pain Society, and influential researchers and medical organizations like those represented on the new Pain commissions--could still pay dividends. But opioids were increasingly seen in exactly the light industry most feared: not as a criminal or legal issue, but. Following the release of the controversial report, Rogers may have felt that his job was done, or realized that being the face of Pharma's pain agenda was a bad thing for an ambitious politician to be. Whatever the cause, in 2011 he pivoted fully to national security and became chair of the House Committee on Intelligence, a post he would hold until 2015, when he left Congress to consult for tech and defense companies. It was a well-timed parachute jump. Within months, the American Pain Foundation self-dissolved following the Senate Finance Committee's announcement that it was into industry influence on opioid advocacy groups. (The American Pain Society would shutter its doors four years later.) In 2012, as Rogers was forcefully turning the page on his congressional career, 52,000 Americans overdosed on opioids, including 2,000 Michiganders. By the time Rogers announced his first Senate campaign in 2023, the groups he'd worked with so closely during the 2000s were gone, but not forgotten. Their names routinely appeared in the $50 billion raft of being settled across the country. "Rogers spent years in Congress pushing a bill that was clearly about training professionals to pump out more opioids, and worked behind the scenes with the companies that contributed to the crisis to get it passed," says Stoltman of the Opioid Policy Institute. "At the end of the day, he was either stupid, an industry stooge, or both." | A guest post by| . Become a Drop Site News Paid Subscriber Drop Site News is reader-supported. name: Gina Hinojosa
subject: A message for Peter
body:
We're 48.9% of the way to our $3M goal before the 9/24 TEC deadline. Here's why I'm writing to you specifically:
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter, this isn't one of our usual campaign updates. I know you hear from my team often, so I wanted to write to you myself today because we've hit a moment in this race that I don't think anyone saw coming a year ago.
**Last week, a Univision/YouGov poll showed Greg Abbott and me tied at 47-47. Not just within the margin. Tied.**
[****](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260915_2_sept.xB3kHe&refcode=em20260915-2123&amount=5&t=1&akid=2123%2E299639%2EBsWO1K)
That's now eight polls this summer with this race inside the margin of error, and last week’s tied poll shows our momentum is only growing. In twelve years and three campaigns for governor, Abbott has never faced anything like this.
But here's what worries me: September 24 is our first public fundraising deadline since June 30. For nearly three months, nobody has seen Abbott's numbers, and we have no idea how much money he's stockpiled to dump on us at the end of this race. This is our second-to-last deadline before Election Day. If Abbott pulls ahead this month, clawing our way back in October will be brutally hard. _**This is the moment when your support in this race matters most, Peter.**_
**That’s why we set a $3 million goal to hit before the September 24 deadline** **— our most ambitious fundraising goal yet — and as of this morning we're 48.9% of the way there.** We need to cross 50% today to stay on track, with just nine days left.
According to our records, you haven't had the chance to chip in yet this month, and I wanted to make sure you heard about where we stand from me before the deadline passes.
Here's what I want you to understand about timing: this race has been a tossup all summer, and Greg Abbott has been sitting on his money in the dark. The window where your grassroots donation can actually shape this race, before he decides how hard to swing against us, is right now. In October, we'll be reacting to what he does. This month, we get to set the terms.
**[So will you make your first contribution of the month right now, even just $5, and help us cross 50% today with nine days to go?](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260915_2_sept.xB3kHe&refcode=em20260915-2123&amount=5&t=3&akid=2123%2E299639%2EBsWO1K)**
[Donate $5 »](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260915_2_sept.xB3kHe&amount=5&refcode=em20260915-2123&t=22&akid=2123%2E299639%2EBsWO1K)
Thank you,
Gina

Dear Friend,**Before you do anything else today, please take a moment to look at the Joshua 1:9 Bookmark pictured above.** This is the bookmark we'll be placing into the hands of children during this year's "See You at the Library Day," and I wanted you to see it for yourself because it represents the message we'll be sharing with thousands of young people across America._Thanks to your support of our mission_ to help parents instill wholesome and Godly values in America’s children... ...this year’s conservative “**See You at the Library Day** ” is shaping up to be our most impactful ever.And BRAVE FOR GOOD hopes to place one **Joshua 1:9** Bookmark into the hands of every little boy and girl who attends.Below are the lessons we’ll be sharing with children at this year’s “See You at the Library Day” to honor of America’s 250th birthday.
---
_1\. Freedom Requires Courage_ We'll remember Thomas Jefferson, the "Father of the Declaration of Independence," and the courage it took to help establish our nation._2\. Great Blessings Require Great Sacrifice_ Children will learn about July 4, 1776, when 56 brave men pledged their "lives, fortunes, and their sacred honor" to secure America's independence._3\. In God We Trust_ And we hope to engrave on every child’s heart at “See You at the Library Day” . . .**IN GOD WE TRUST**
---
**[Friend](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyckc-KnEAQxp-mvbX0P7U9eJjFcRnIZMMYNuTUlHbpNFFb7HYkbx8m7L7AQp1-VBX8vu_X1VzBTW4Zv8OMlQvBbMEcCBtOGEK8wxIPfyD-CXDAXyOYyCkrKc8M9NE90ChIbJUJrgedYMULXaqyKHme3CthRaezIYMO1CBLKzMpS8gL_pyhGBJXPf-xkmdcq4yrlAmV2x5YqZF1fSeJYvtqIWLqluAsht77dfWTi64Pqd_GZKruMa6ByBMRDRFNwH7fMIUFrY9p72cimm6DB9LBb3T03hLRrDCoLmfSdlRxC1QxW1CtZUmtFIUGIbjWkshmj7MJft96JLK-nd-JyJ9oRuv2mcj6fD1dvn3AHuYV3LgQWX9YKfNSv5qX5vXN3M7v5v-yaX--3X5z-uNEL237eeqXiEsksr60Lf3MJNkqux5umlzIC6LYOIObnkpJ_GJRj0r8CwAA___i9Z35)[, America’s children need to hear that message from us because today’s “educators” and librarians are radicals!](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyckc-KnEAQxp-mvbX0P7U9eJjFcRnIZMMYNuTUlHbpNFFb7HYkbx8m7L7AQp1-VBX8vu_X1VzBTW4Zv8OMlQvBbMEcCBtOGEK8wxIPfyD-CXDAXyOYyCkrKc8M9NE90ChIbJUJrgedYMULXaqyKHme3CthRaezIYMO1CBLKzMpS8gL_pyhGBJXPf-xkmdcq4yrlAmV2x5YqZF1fSeJYvtqIWLqluAsht77dfWTi64Pqd_GZKruMa6ByBMRDRFNwH7fMIUFrY9p72cimm6DB9LBb3T03hLRrDCoLmfSdlRxC1QxW1CtZUmtFIUGIbjWkshmj7MJft96JLK-nd-JyJ9oRuv2mcj6fD1dvn3AHuYV3LgQWX9YKfNSv5qX5vXN3M7v5v-yaX--3X5z-uNEL237eeqXiEsksr60Lf3MJNkqux5umlzIC6LYOIObnkpJ_GJRj0r8CwAA___i9Z35)[](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyckc-KnEAQxp-mvbX0P7U9eJjFcRnIZMMYNuTUlHbpNFFb7HYkbx8m7L7AQp1-VBX8vu_X1VzBTW4Zv8OMlQvBbMEcCBtOGEK8wxIPfyD-CXDAXyOYyCkrKc8M9NE90ChIbJUJrgedYMULXaqyKHme3CthRaezIYMO1CBLKzMpS8gL_pyhGBJXPf-xkmdcq4yrlAmV2x5YqZF1fSeJYvtqIWLqluAsht77dfWTi64Pqd_GZKruMa6ByBMRDRFNwH7fMIUFrY9p72cimm6DB9LBb3T03hLRrDCoLmfSdlRxC1QxW1CtZUmtFIUGIbjWkshmj7MJft96JLK-nd-JyJ9oRuv2mcj6fD1dvn3AHuYV3LgQWX9YKfNSv5qX5vXN3M7v5v-yaX--3X5z-uNEL237eeqXiEsksr60Lf3MJNkqux5umlzIC6LYOIObnkpJ_GJRj0r8CwAA___i9Z35)** Back when you were growing up, you may remember lazy Saturdays at the library with a kind but stern librarian.She would fill your mind with classics like Pat the Bunny and The Little Engine That Could. And eventually you got old enough to roam by yourself and discover adventures like the Three Musketeers, Treasure Island and Charlotte’s Web. But today, all that has changed.Instead of filling children with wholesome stories, the president of the American Library Association (ALA) says libraries should be used to address ‘systemic racism’ and elevate ‘BIPOC and LGBTQIA+ writers and voices.’ Radical librarians call Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and To Kill a Mockingbird “racist.” They’ve stripped Laura Ingalls Wilder’s name from a prestigious book award because of her“problematic’ Little House series.And they bring in men wearing full makeup, dresses, and high heels for “Drag Queen Story Hours” where books like these are read to children of all ages...
---
| | | _A is for Activist._ An ABC board book for “families who want their kids to grow up in a space that is unapologetic about activism, environmental justice, civil rights, LGBTQ rights, andeverything else that activists believe in and fight for.” _Woke Baby_. “For all the littlest progressives, waking up to seize a new day of justice and activism. Woke babies raise their fists in the air. Wokebabies cry out for justice. Woke babies grow up to change the world.”
---
_Prince and Knight_. The “premier queer-friendly fairy tale” about a prince who marries a knight instead of a princess._And The Hips on the Drag Queens Go Swish, Swish, Swish_. A “family-friendly celebration ofdrag” that encourages children to “work it.”
---

_**Cliff 's Note:**_
##### Here is something I did not have on my bingo card. Over the weekend, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk -- three men who have spent years telling us the race is the point -- all said out loud that somebody needs to slow the race down. When the arsonists start asking for a fire code, you pay attention.
##### The White House called it a Chinese hoax.
##### David Shuster spent this week on what happens next, and the back half of this piece is the part I would pay for: what the people inside that building are quietly telling him to do about it, and why he probably will not. That reporting is for members.

_**-- Cliff**_
* * *
_**by David Shuster**_
In golf, it is a one foot putt. In basketball, it is called a wide-open layup. . In soccer or hockey, it is the shot taken from three feet away at an empty net.
Whatever the terminology, Donald Trump now has one of the easiest political plays imaginable sitting in front of him.
It is also a matter involving the continued existence of the human race.
And yet there is every indication that Trump may find a way to miss.
The subject is artificial intelligence.
This past weekend, the leading competing titans of the A.I. industry each said A.I. research needs to slow down.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f0487620-de50-44af-aa08-78c54227d679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for governments to "pace" frontier AI development, arguing that capabilities are advancing too quickly for existing safeguards to keep up. Open AI's Sam Altman said he agrees and supports greater coordination. Elon Musk weighed in and said Amodei and Altman are correct and that there needs to be government mandated and enforced restraint. Other prominent AI figures are also advocating for independent safety evaluations and government involvement.
Blue Amp Media is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.CQu-CfQy-c_3rLKtsujW5Nhh8ezsUns8yhTXGcx78R4?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=215744694)
Front line AI researchers have been issuing dire warnings for months. Most recently and prominently, 27-year-old researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and declared, in a now viral social media post and several interviews, that OpenAI and Anthropic have been working irresponsibly. Coxon declared that people building the technology genuinely believe it could kill everybody by the end of the decade.
For a primer on the threats of superintelligence and the key issues, please read this column by my colleague [Lawrence Winnerman](https://open.substack.com/users/314034871-lawrence-winnerman?utm_source=mentions) .
## [Welcome to the P(Doom) Economy](https://substack.com/redirect/eb12da17-9f67-437e-81e2-81eb4caaad3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
---
| | [Lawrence Winnerman](https://substack.com/profile/314034871-lawrence-winnerman) and [Blue Amp Media](https://substack.com/profile/312330913-blue-amp-media)| | *
---|---|---
| Sep 12
[](https://substack.com/redirect/eb12da17-9f67-437e-81e2-81eb4caaad3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
[Cliff's Note:](https://substack.com/redirect/eb12da17-9f67-437e-81e2-81eb4caaad3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
| [| Read full story
---](https://substack.com/redirect/eb12da17-9f67-437e-81e2-81eb4caaad3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
As Lawrence notes, some of the people engaged in this race think the chances are high that it will trigger a human extinction event.
The question is no longer whether A.I. will transform civilization. That part is settled. It will. The question is whether civilization will remain in charge of the transformation and live to use it.
I believe that A.I. could produce miracles. It may accelerate the conquest of cancer, transform medicine, improve education, increase productivity beyond anything previously imagined, and solve problems that have tortured humankind for centuries. It may someday make the ordinary human workweek look like an eccentric historical curiosity.
Great.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f0487620-de50-44af-aa08-78c54227d679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
But do we have to try and reach this paradise by conducting the most consequential technological experiment in human history according to the business philosophy of a Las Vegas casino? Build faster. Deploy faster. Beat the other gambler. And if you lose, oh well. There is always another table. Except in this case, perhaps everybody dies.
The sensible proposal is not to ban A.I. Nor is it to strangle technological development or voluntarily hand America's technological lead to Beijing. The sensible proposal is considerably less dramatic: establish rules for the most powerful systems so this is not a race in which nobody can afford to brake.
That means independent testing. Reporting requirements. Serious security standards. Restrictions on deploying systems that fail clearly defined safety evaluations. And legal mechanisms permitting competing companies to share certain safety information without being treated as conspirators against the sacred interests of commerce.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.CQu-CfQy-c_3rLKtsujW5Nhh8ezsUns8yhTXGcx78R4?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=215744694)
None of this is exotic or extreme
We already regulate banks, airplanes, nuclear reactors, pharmaceuticals and other things that can produce unpleasant consequences when operated carelessly. Civilization has occasionally learned that "move fast and break things" is not an adequate philosophy when the thing being broken happens to be civilization.
The central problem is a simple one.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f0487620-de50-44af-aa08-78c54227d679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Every leading A.I. company may rationally believe that slowing down would be safer. But each company also fears that if it slows down while its competitors continue racing, it will lose the race.
So everyone in the A.I. industry accelerates.
This is not necessarily because everyone is insane. It is because everyone is responding rationally to an irrational set of incentives involving trillions of dollars in potential revenue.
That is precisely the kind of problem government regulations exist to solve.
The strongest objection, as Donald Trump has pointed to, involves China. If the U.S. slows down, would Beijing? A unilateral American retreat could surrender an important economic and strategic advantage. And as Trump said recently, "whoever wins the A.I. race wins."
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f0487620-de50-44af-aa08-78c54227d679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
But regulation and technological leadership are not opposites. The United States could seek international agreements governing the most dangerous capabilities while continuing to invest aggressively in research, computing, semiconductor manufacturing, robotics, and less hazardous applications. Indeed, American leadership may be more valuable if it produces standards that other countries ultimately adopt.
The easiest part of all of this involves U.S. domestic politics.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.CQu-CfQy-c_3rLKtsujW5Nhh8ezsUns8yhTXGcx78R4?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=215744694)
Trump's approval/disapproval rating is now the worst of any U.S. President in fifty years. And in his handling of Artificial Intelligence, a new [University of Massachusetts Amherst poll](https://substack.com/redirect/97db6296-1c0d-474a-8a85-50a7cfddb90a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) just found that 23 percent of American voters say Trump has handled AI well, compared with 57 percent who say he has handled it poorly. That's a minus 34. Among independent voters, Trump is at minus 61.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f0487620-de50-44af-aa08-78c54227d679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
According to a poll conducted by CBS News, 54 percent of voters would prefer a candidate who opposes new data centers in their area, compared to 15 percent who would prefer one who supports building them.
Even if Americans don't believe A.I. will extinguish humanity, most voters believe AI will bring them financial ruin. The U-Mass poll found 64 percent of Americans think AI will reduce the number of jobs, while just 19 percent say it will create more.
There are some Trump White House staff who see the polling, appreciate the dire challenges facing Trump's GOP in the mid-term elections, and also worry about the existential threat that A.I. may pose. These aides have reportedly advised Trump to deliver a prime-time speech to the nation, declare that certain aspects of A.I. could threaten humanity, and announce specific A.I. regulations the industry is requesting. Trump could also claim he is saving humanity from extinction. And in this case, Trump would probably be correct.
