Trump’s voter suppression scheme was stopped (for now)
| | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139275225/646814481/2140832878?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDEvMS84OTQxMiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIzYTU4NjkwMS01NWIxLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=02AZUz_jCLDkc4DYJFSakPhoQBkjdmf3zhljQI35RqU=&emci=309c1f05-4ab1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=3a586901-55b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=9818364)
---

| | Yesterday, the Supreme Court **shut down** Trump's scheme to disrupt mail-in voting. The U.S. Postal Service is now **prohibited** from carrying out Trump's illegal order that would have caused hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots to never be sent to registered voters. [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139275226/646814482/-2044921950?refcode=2026-09-15-usps&recurring=0&amount=&amounts=10,30,50,100,200&refcode2=3a586901-55b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDEvMS84OTQxMiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIzYTU4NjkwMS01NWIxLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=02AZUz_jCLDkc4DYJFSakPhoQBkjdmf3zhljQI35RqU=) As a longtime champion of Oregon's vote-by-mail system, I'm relieved by this ruling. Trump's order would've caused nothing but chaos for us — and many other states. But I'm also not complacent. Trump will surely try something like this again in advance of 2028, and I expect more Hail Mary attempts by him in these next 7 weeks to make Americans feel unsure and unsafe about voting in 2026. If your vote didn't matter, Trump wouldn't be working so hard to suppress it. **I'm going to fight like hell to ensure any scheme by Donald Trump to make it harder to vote in November dies the death it so richly deserves.** I've proposed a bill to allow _everyone_ in the country to vote by mail. The U.S. Postal Service is now prohibited from carrying out Trump's illegal order that would have caused hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots to never be sent to registered voters. = As a longtime champion of Oregon's vote-by-mail system, I'm relieved by this ruling. Trump's order would've caused nothing but chaos for us — and many other states. But I'm also not complacent. Trump will surely try something like this again in advance of 2028, and I expect more Hail Mary attempts by him in these next 7 weeks to make Americans feel unsure and unsafe about voting in 2026. If your vote didn't matter, Trump wouldn't be working so hard to suppress it. I'm going to fight like hell to ensure any scheme by Donald Trump to make it harder to vote in November dies the death it so richly deserves. I've proposed a bill to allow everyone in the country to vote by mail. It's convenient, cost-effective, and secure. Trump's war with Iran isn't just costing lives and driving up gas prices. It's draining the actual weapons America needs to deter a far more dangerous conflict — with China. Here's what I laid out. The United States has reportedly burned through almost half of its global supply of Tomahawk cruise missiles. We've used "virtually all" of our Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles. Patriot missile stockpiles are down by two-thirds. THAAD interceptors are down by half. Defense planners call this "magazine depth" — and ours is disappearing faster than we can rebuild it. **Why does that matter beyond Iran?** Because America's entire strategy for preventing war with China depends on Beijing believing that aggression will fail. That deterrence only works if our military capability, our alliances, and our resolve are visibly intact. Every missile we burn through in an open-ended, strategy-free war with Iran is a missile we don't have if a real crisis erupts in the Pacific. I made the case plainly: We are sliding toward a war we are not prepared for, while distracted by one we never needed to fight this way. Here's the thing, though. Writing the op-ed matters. Getting the argument right matters. But none of it changes anything by itself. What actually changes this is electing Democrats who will demand accountability, follow through on real oversight, and have the backbone to stand up to reckless, strategy-free warmongering — not just write about it, but do something about it in Washington. That's exactly why I built Equal Opportunity Now. There is a reason people like Zohran Mamdani. Actually, there are quite a few. He talks about government as though its purpose is to make ordinary people's lives better, puts that talk into action consistently and unapologetically, and seems genuinely delighted by both the people and the work.
His administration has financed more than 12,000 affordable homes as part of a five-year, $22 billion housing investment. It launched New York City's first free 2-K program. In August, it eliminated the remaining weekly child-care co-pays for roughly 22,000 low-income families already receiving assistance. This month, it announced a modernization of the city's antiquated school procurement system projected to save more than $100 million.
He goes to Rikers Island and breaks his fast with incarcerated people and corrections officers alike. He tells Jewish New Yorkers that their safety is his responsibility. He talks about halal-cart vendors whose knees hurt after standing all day, construction workers in steel-toed boots, tenants struggling to make rent, and mothers trying to get their children to school and themselves to work.
When people told the first Muslim mayor of New York that his religion made his presence inappropriate at the twenty-fifth anniversary of September 11, he didn't make the day about the insult to him. He spent the weeks beforehand meeting firefighters, survivors, and victims' families, addressing the continuing health consequences of Ground Zero, and releasing 170,000 city documents concerning air quality that had been withheld from the public for years. Then he showed up to mourn with his city.
You don't have to know anything about Islam to appreciate the pattern: **service, stewardship, mercy, justice, truthfulness, attention to people with less power, and an understanding that holding authority creates obligations toward everyone -- including people who didn't vote for you, don't share your religion, or actively dislike you.**
But here is the part I suspect many Americans don't know: those aren't merely values that Mamdani happens to possess while also happening to be Muslim. They are **deeply recognizable Islamic values of leadership**. Islam has names for them.
And at a moment when an astonishing amount of American political discourse is once again trying to convince people that a Muslim practicing his religion in public is inherently threatening -- _Sharia. Jihad. Islamist._ perfectly legitimate Arabic words, stripped of meaning and repurposed as alarm bells -- it seems worth actually talking about what the religion teaches.
We have a rather good case study running New York City.

## _Amanah_ : You Have Been Entrusted With Something
Mamdani keeps talking about public office in a particular way -- not as something he has won and therefore possesses, but as something he has been entrusted with. At his inauguration, he promised to govern "expansively and audaciously," but the more revealing promise was simpler: whether New Yorkers agreed with him or not, he said, he would protect them, celebrate with them, grieve with them, and never hide from them. That's not really a policy platform. It's a definition of the office.
Islam has a word for the idea underneath it: _amanah_. A trust -- something valuable, placed temporarily into your hands, carrying obligations precisely because it does not ultimately belong to you. One of the Qur'an's central instructions concerning authority is remarkably direct: _" Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice."_ (Qur'an 4:58) Notice the language: between people. Not between Muslims. The obligation is not sectarian.
And _amanah_ isn't merely generosity with other people's money you've been entrusted with. It is responsible stewardship of it. That's why the boring procurement story may actually be one of my favorite examples. Finding a way to save New York's schools more than $100 million by fixing a procurement system "built for 2006" doesn't make for soaring political theater. But being compassionate while carelessly wasting what you've been entrusted with isn't _amanah_. Taking responsibility for the machinery of government -- including the boring parts -- is.

## '_Adl_ : Justice, Even When It Costs Your Side
There is another pattern in Mamdani's politics: his own community's claim to belonging has never required somebody else's exclusion. He has spoken unapologetically about Muslims belonging in the halls of power while making an equally explicit commitment to protecting Jewish New Yorkers from antisemitism. His political vocabulary continually widens the circle -- immigrants, Black women, trans New Yorkers, single mothers, workers, tenants, people who voted against him.
Islam has a word for the principle underneath that: _' adl_, justice. And the Qur'anic standard for it is considerably more demanding than "be fair to your friends." _" Stand firmly for justice, as witnesses for God, even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or your close relatives."_ (Qur'an 4:135) Another passage goes further: _" Do not let the hatred of a people lead you away from justice. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness."_ (Qur'an 5:8)
Put those together and you get something quite different from identity politics in its crudest form. Islam does not say: acquire power so your people finally get their turn. It says that acquiring power increases your obligation to justice -- including toward people who are not yours, people you dislike, and people whose interests may conflict with your own. Power is supposed to expand the moral circle, not shrink it.

## _Rahmah_ : The Humanity of Both the Prisoner and the Guard
Then there is Rikers Island. During Ramadan, Mamdani became the first New York City mayor to break the fast there. He prayed and ate alongside incarcerated Muslims, many of them still awaiting trial, and Muslim corrections officers. Think about the political symbolism available to him in that room: prisoners on one side, guards on the other, the state and the people confined by the state, breaking bread together, along with their mayor.
Asked why he went, Mamdani didn't reach for a criminal-justice talking point. "This is me just being a Muslim New Yorker," he said. "There are some for whom that is a political act." A sitting United States senator responded by posting a photograph of Mamdani's Rikers iftar next to an image of the burning Twin Towers. Mamdani kept going -- seventeen public iftars that Ramadan, from City Hall to a mosque in Jamaica, Queens.
Islam has a word for the instinct underneath this, too: _rahmah_ , mercy -- not mercy in the weak sense of refusing judgment or pretending harm doesn't matter, but mercy as a governing disposition. It's the refusal to let an institution, an offense, a uniform, a political category, or somebody's usefulness to you exhaust your understanding of their humanity. The prisoner is human. The guard is human. The mayor's obligation to recognize that does not disappear because recognizing both at once makes for messier politics. Human dignity comes before the label the state has stamped on you.
## Caring for the People who've been Made Powerless
There is another Arabic word worth knowing: _mustad 'afin_. It appears repeatedly in the Qur'an, and it means something close to those who have been made weak -- people rendered vulnerable or powerless by the conditions around them. Poverty, vulnerability and marginalization are not always simply characteristics people happen to possess. Sometimes people have been made powerless by systems built by people with considerably more power.
Mamdani's politics is unusually concrete about who government exists to notice. Not "working families" or "the middle class" as political abstractions, but the halal food-cart vendor, the construction worker, the tenant, the aging grandmother, the single mother trying to get a child to school and still make it to work on time.
His administration's first citywide Racial Equity Plan makes some of that attention measurable: goals across housing, maternal mortality, education, employment and transportation, accompanied by an explicit invitation to New Yorkers to hold the administration accountable for meeting them. That is _amanah_ again, in another key -- your attention, from a position of power, deliberately flowing toward people with the least power to reward you for giving it.

## Tell the Truth. Especially to Power.
There is another dimension of Islamic leadership worth addressing, because mercy without moral courage can become mere politeness. Islam does not only tell people to recognize injustice. **It places an obligation on them to confront it.** The Prophet Muhammad put it with startling directness: _" Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart -- and that is the weakest of faith."_ (Sahih Muslim 49)
Look at the hierarchy. If you possess the power to stop something wrong, use it. If you don't, speak against it. And if even speaking is beyond your capacity, at minimum do not let power persuade your conscience that wrong has become right.
That sheds some light on another feature of Mamdani's political style: he can be remarkably unwilling to euphemize. He has said publicly that Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, describing him as the architect of a genocide against Palestinians and pointing to the International Criminal Court's warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.
But the more revealing part is the principle Mamdani says he is applying. He has also called the atrocities of October 7 a horrific war crime, and asked about the apparent contradiction, his answer was essentially that there isn't one: **humanity is universal.** "We cannot pick and choose which crimes against humanity we oppose," he said. ICC warrants should be treated consistently, whether they concern Netanyahu, Yahya Sinwar, Vladimir Putin, or anyone else. That is almost a case study in Qur'an 5:8 -- do not let your hatred of one people cause you to abandon justice, or for that matter, your allegiance to another.
Mamdani has also been careful about the distinction between moral condemnation and lawful authority, insisting that he can say what he believes to be true about Netanyahu while acknowledging the legal limits on what a New York mayor can actually do.
Say what you believe to be true. Do what is actually within your authority. Don't pretend to possess powers you don't. And don't pretend not to see wrongdoing simply because the person responsible is powerful. That is a recognizable Islamic moral posture.
But the harder test came much closer to home: his own office. For twenty-five years, New Yorkers exposed to the toxic dust of September 11 fought to understand what their government knew about the air they were breathing. In September, Mamdani's administration settled two longstanding lawsuits over those records and released an initial cache of more than 170,000 pages, including records survivors, first responders and advocates had sought for years. And the mayor did not sanitize what they contained. "These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it and how they acted to limit liability," he said.
They include records of asbestos appearing throughout environmental testing and discussions within the Giuliani administration about health hazards and potential liability. Mamdani's administration committed $34 million to a public portal where the records can be examined freely, with substantially more documents scheduled for release.
Why does that belong in an essay about Islamic leadership? Because the public's trust is also an _amanah_ , and **truth is part of what has been entrusted**. Islam is exceptionally severe about rulers who deceive the people they govern. In a hadith recorded in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the Prophet warns that a ruler whom God entrusts with people and who dies while deceiving them faces an extraordinary condemnation: Paradise is forbidden to him. That is not treated as a minor lapse of political ethics. It is a fundamental betrayal of the trust itself.
Look, then, at the choice facing the new administration. It possessed information damaging to the institution it now controlled. That institution had spent years resisting disclosure. The people had a right to know. Mamdani, the first among those who've held that office, gave the truth back to them -- almost a literal enactment of _amanah_ : restore what has been entrusted to you to those to whom it belongs.
That connects two episodes that otherwise look completely different. Calling Netanyahu a war criminal means speaking clearly about someone extraordinarily powerful. Releasing the 9/11 records means exposing wrongdoing by the government Mamdani himself now leads.
Different circumstances, same underlying proposition: power does not acquire a right to comfortable lies merely because exposing the truth is inconvenient.
If you can change the wrong with your hand, change it. If you cannot, speak. And if you are entrusted with the truth itself, give it back.

## And Yes, Let's Talk About Sharia
This is approximately where somebody on cable television starts shouting _It 'S sHaRiA!!!!_, which is revealing, because most Americans encountering that word in political rhetoric **have never actually been told what it means.**
Shari'ah does not mean "Muslims take over the government and make everybody Muslim." The word originally evokes _a path leading to water_ -- a way toward the source of life. In Islam, it came to mean the divinely guided path for how a person should live. It refers broadly to the Islamic path of moral and religious life -- encompassing worship, fasting, charity, marriage, contracts, inheritance, treatment of neighbors, obligations toward the poor, personal conduct, and, yes, traditions of jurisprudence and governance, when the societal situation supports them.
Is Zohran Mamdani trying to make New Yorkers live under Islamic religious law? **No**. There is no evidence he has ever proposed anything resembling that. The First Amendment and the U.S. Constitution he's sworn to uphold wouldn't permit it anyway. But there is an even more interesting answer: **Islam itself wouldn 't permit what his critics are imagining, either.**
The Qur'an says it with startling economy: _" There is no compulsion in religion."_ (Qur'an 2:256) That wasn't invented by twenty-first-century Muslims trying to make Islam sound palatable to liberal Americans. Classical Qur'anic commentators have understood the verse as a prohibition against forcing people to become Muslim for well more than a millennium.
The Qur'an elsewhere asks Muhammad himself: if God had willed, everyone could have believed -- given that, _" Would you then compel people to become believers?"_ (Qur'an 10:99), asking directly whether Muhammad would seek to override God's own wisdom and purpose in creating different communities of faith.
**Of course not.**
And the Qur'an does something even more interesting when discussing Jews and Christians. In chapter 5, it asks why Jews are bringing disputes to Muhammad when they already have the Torah, containing God's judgment. It tells the Christians, people of the Gospel, to judge according to what God revealed to them in it. And then it says: _" For each of you We have appointed a law and a way. Had God willed, He could have made you one community... so compete with one another in good works."_ (Qur'an 5:48) The Qur'an itself recognizes religious communities living alongside one another without requiring that their religious laws become identical.
That principle became something recognizable throughout Islamic history: **legal pluralism.** Muslim governments were certainly not modern liberal democracies, and the historical record contains hierarchies, restrictions, injustices and episodes of persecution that shouldn't be airbrushed away. But Jewish and Christian communities commonly retained their own religious institutions and jurisdiction over significant areas of communal and family life, alongside the Muslim courts and public order. This isn't a modern reinterpretation invented because pluralism became fashionable. It has roots at the beginning.
**Most Americans, myself included, were never taught any of this.** An entire civilization -- centuries of a way of life across huge portions of the planet, giving rise to astonishing developments in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, technology, and philosophy that seeded the European Renaissance -- completely erased from our textbooks. (What a deprivation of humanity's moral and intellectual inheritance.) For our purposes here, three moments in Islamic history are worth knowing.

### Medina: One City, More Than One Faith
When Muhammad became the political leader of Medina, he did not require its Jewish communities to become Muslim. The document traditionally known as the Constitution or Charter of Medina established agreements among the city's different communities concerning mutual defense, obligations, security and dispute resolution while explicitly recognizing religious distinction.
The exact constitutional meaning of that document is debated by historians, and we shouldn't pretend seventh-century Medina was a modern liberal republic. It wasn't. But the underlying fact is difficult to miss: **Muhammad, the founder of Islam, governed a city containing communities that did not share his religion, and their continued religious existence was recognized rather than erased.** The Qur'an's own language about Jews judging by Torah and Christians by Gospel belongs to that same world.
Islam **did not** require everyone living under Muslim political authority to become Muslim.
### Jerusalem: What Conquest Could Have Looked Like -- and Didn't
Then consider Jerusalem. When the Muslim armies took the city in 638, Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab came personally to receive its surrender. This was a conquest -- we don't need to sanitize that word. What matters is what happened _next_. The Christian population was not massacred. Their churches were **not** systematically destroyed. Their holy places remained Christian places of worship; indeed, the protection Umar granted Jerusalem's Christians and their churches would be invoked by later Muslim authorities as a reason Christians' sacred spaces could not simply be confiscated.
And something else happened. Under Byzantine Christian rule, Jews had been barred from Jerusalem. **After the Muslim conquest, Jewish life returned to the city.** Jewish historical sources themselves remember Umar as permitting Jews to reestablish a presence in Jerusalem after centuries of exclusion.
That comparison becomes especially uncomfortable when we move forward several centuries. When Christian Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, the conquest culminated in the mass killing of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Contemporary accounts differ wildly about the number killed, but not about the reality of the slaughter.
### Al-Andalus: Not Utopia. Something More Interesting.
And then there is Muslim Spain. Al-Andalus gets romanticized sometimes as an interfaith paradise where Muslims, Christians and Jews all held hands and invented algebra together. History is messier than that -- there were legal inequalities, conflicts, periods of persecution, rulers considerably better than others.
But something extraordinary nevertheless happened there. For centuries, Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in the same civilization and participated in overlapping intellectual, commercial, medical, diplomatic and cultural worlds. Jewish intellectual life flourished spectacularly during important periods of Muslim rule. Christians continued living and worshiping there. Arabic became a language of scholarship crossing religious boundaries.
And non-Muslims didn't merely survive at the margins -- some rose astonishingly high. Hasdai ibn Shaprut, a Jewish physician and scholar in tenth-century Cordoba, became one of Caliph Abd al-Rahman III's most important diplomats and officials, directing customs administration and conducting diplomatic negotiations with Christian kingdoms on the caliph's behalf. A century later, Samuel ha-Nagid -- Jewish poet, Talmudic scholar and statesman -- became vizier of Granada and commanded Muslim armies.
Pause on that one: **a Jewish religious scholar became one of the most powerful officials in a Muslim kingdom and commanded its Muslim soldiers.**
That does not prove medieval Islam secretly invented twenty-first-century egalitarian democracy. It proves something much simpler and harder to square with the cartoon version of Islamic civilization Americans are routinely sold: **religious difference and Muslim political leadership were not inherently incompatible with civic collaboration, intellectual exchange, communal autonomy, or even extraordinary positions of public trust.**
There is a historical lineage here -- Medina, Jerusalem, Cordoba and Granada. Different centuries, different political systems, imperfect human beings producing imperfect societies. But the underlying idea keeps appearing: Muslim leadership does not require everybody being led to become Muslim.
Which brings us back to New York.

## His Muslimness Doesn't Need an Apology
For decades, prominent American Muslims in public life have often been pushed toward one of two performances: minimize the faith until everyone is reassured that you're harmless, or allow your Muslim identity to become the entire political story.
Mamdani does neither. He fasts while running America's largest city. He says _Assalamu alaikum_ in public. He visits mosques. He was sworn in at midnight on his grandfather's Qur'an and ceremonially on a centuries-old Qur'an from the Schomburg collection that once belonged to the Black Puerto Rican historian Arturo Schomburg. And then he goes back to talking about buses and child care and housing and garbage and procurement reform.
That is genuine normalization. His faith neither disappears nor demands dominion. It is simply there, forming the person exercising power.
And perhaps that's why the anti-Sharia hysteria is so revealing. Christians are allowed to enter public life shaped by "love thy neighbor." Jews are allowed to arrive carrying centuries of Jewish ethical thought. Secular humanists are allowed to possess deeply held convictions about dignity, equality and human flourishing. Of course a Muslim public official is shaped by Islam. _Why wouldn 't he be?_
The relevant constitutional question isn't whether his faith influences his moral character. It is whether he uses government to impose that faith on everyone else. Mamdani doesn't. And the irony is that the religious tradition his haters panic over, actually contains **explicit instructions against religious compulsion and a long history of governing communities in which multiple religions continued to exist.**
A Muslim does not become threatening because he arrives in public life carrying a moral tradition. The question is what that tradition teaches him to do with power, and how faithfully he exercises it.

## The Hardest Test Yet
Which brings us to September 11.
A Muslim mayor of New York presiding over the twenty-fifth anniversary of the attacks is about as symbolically loaded a situation as American public life can produce. Some critics -- including a former mayor of the city -- argued openly that Mamdani's faith itself made his presence at the memorial inappropriate.
Think about what that claim actually does: it collapses "Muslim" back into "the men who did this," as if nearly two million Muslim Americans haven't spent the intervening quarter-century living, working, raising families, serving in uniform, becoming doctors and teachers and firefighters and public servants, and burying their own dead in this country.
**Mamdani had every moral right to be furious.** But his response was _not_ to center his own injury. He went to firehouses and stood with the FDNY as it remembered the members it lost. He stood with police officers and their families, and joined an interfaith memorial service at St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church.
And when he spoke about September 11, he spoke about New Yorkers. He told the story of an older man falling as the dust cloud raced toward him, and the people fleeing alongside him stopping, turning around, putting their arms beneath him, and lifting him back onto his feet. He spoke about the flotilla of boats that converged on Lower Manhattan after the Coast Guard called for help -- people carrying strangers, people helping children and elderly New Yorkers aboard, a city refusing to leave people behind. Those who attacked New York, Mamdani said, believed they could break the city at its fractures. They were wrong.
That is an extraordinary thing for America's first Muslim mayor to say at the twenty-fifth anniversary of an attack that transformed Muslim life in this country -- not because he apologized for being Muslim, which he didn't, and not because he demanded that the day acknowledge what happened to Muslims afterward, which he didn't need to.
He simply fulfilled the responsibility of the office he holds: these people suffered, this is my city, I am their mayor, I will remember with them.
New Yorkers noticed the difference in his performance and character. A Suffolk University poll released that same week found him with strong approval numbers and a majority saying he'd exceeded their expectations in office, with nearly three-quarters of voters saying he should attend the commemoration despite demands that he stay away.
Before reading this essay, perhaps you would simply have called his response _**grace**_. Now you know another word for what you're seeing: _amanah_. His critics looked at a Muslim standing at Ground Zero and concluded that Islam was the problem.
Look again. **Islam may be part of the reason he understood how profound his obligation was to be there.**

## Let's Not Canonize Him
There is an important caution here. Eight months is not a mayoral term. Mamdani is a politician, not a saint, and Islam itself gives us particularly good reasons to resist confusing those categories. Leadership is tested across the whole stewardship, especially once stewardship becomes inconvenient -- when allies want favors, when budgets force painful tradeoffs, when a mistake needs admitting and admitting it is politically expensive, when somebody you despise deserves justice, when popularity and principle stop pointing in the same direction.
New York will test Mamdani on all of that. It should.
But the pattern so far is not nothing.
_Amanah_ : power as trust.
_' Adl_: justice beyond tribe.
_Rahmah_ : mercy as a way of encountering other human beings.
Concern for the _mustad 'afin_: attention to those power has rendered powerless.
The duty to _confront wrongdoing_ : act where you have power, speak where you do not, and refuse inwardly to call evil good.
And _no compulsion in religion_ : faith expressed through character rather than forced through the state.
And there is one more thing, which isn't a category of jurisprudence but may matter almost as much: **he smiles.** He jokes about chai and biryani and the outrageous price of New York coffee. He has talked about his grandmother teaching him that following the Prophet's example included smiling at people.
There is something genuinely attractive about an Islam presented to America not primarily as prohibition, grievance, apologetics or theological argument, but simply lived: feed people, know your neighbors, protect the vulnerable, keep your promises, don't waste what you've been entrusted with, stand for justice even when it costs your own side, tell the truth when power would rather you didn't, recognize the humanity of the prisoner and the guard, protect people whose religion is different from yours, show up when your neighbors mourn, and smile at people.
Maybe the most useful thing Mamdani is doing for Americans' understanding of Islam isn't explaining Islam at all. He's just **practicing it where everyone can see him**. None of this requires New York to become Muslim. It requires a Muslim entrusted with New York to take seriously what his religion asks of _**him**_.
And perhaps, after twenty-five years in which Americans have been trained to hear Arabic words and imagine danger, there is something quietly corrective about learning a few different ones.
_Amanah. 'Adl. Rahmah._
Trust. Justice. Mercy.
You already knew what they looked like. Now you know some of their names.

An introduction to the Islamic principles behind his approach to power, justice, mercy, and public service. | | | Sep 15 | | | | | | | | | | | | There is a reason people like Zohran Mamdani. Actually, there are quite a few. He talks about government as though its purpose is to make ordinary people's lives better, puts that talk into action consistently and unapologetically, and seems genuinely delighted by both the people and the work. His administration has financed more than 12,000 affordable homes as part of a five-year, $22 billion housing investment. It launched New York City's first free 2-K program. In August, it eliminated the remaining weekly child-care co-pays for roughly 22,000 low-income families already receiving assistance. This month, it announced a modernization of the city's antiquated school procurement system projected to save more than $100 million. He goes to Rikers Island and breaks his fast with incarcerated people and corrections officers alike. He tells Jewish New Yorkers that their safety is his responsibility. He talks about halal-cart vendors whose knees hurt after standing all day, construction workers in steel-toed boots, tenants struggling to make rent, and mothers trying to get their children to school and themselves to work. When people told the first Muslim mayor of New York that his religion made his presence inappropriate at the twenty-fifth anniversary of September 11, he didn't make the day about the insult to him. He spent the weeks beforehand meeting firefighters, survivors, and victims' families, addressing the continuing health consequences of Ground Zero, and releasing 170,000 city documents concerning air quality that had been withheld from the public for years. Then he showed up to mourn with his city. You don't have to know anything about Islam to appreciate the pattern: service, stewardship, mercy, justice, truthfulness, attention to people with less power, and an understanding that holding authority creates obligations toward everyone -- including people who didn't vote for you, don't share your religion, or actively dislike you. But here is the part I suspect many Americans don't know: those aren't merely values that Mamdani happens to possess while also happening to be Muslim. They are deeply recognizable Islamic values of leadership. Islam has names for them. And at a moment when an astonishing amount of American political discourse is once again trying to convince people that a Muslim practicing his religion in public is inherently threatening -- Sharia. Jihad. Islamist. perfectly legitimate Arabic words, stripped of meaning and repurposed as alarm bells -- it seems worth actually talking about what the religion teaches. We have a rather good case study running New York City. Amanah : You Have Been Entrusted With Something Mamdani keeps talking about public office in a particular way -- not as something he has won and therefore possesses, but as something he has been entrusted with. At his inauguration, he promised to govern "expansively and audaciously," but the more revealing promise was simpler: whether New Yorkers agreed with him or not, he said, he would protect them, celebrate with them, grieve with them, and never hide from them. That's not really a policy platform. It's a definition of the office. Islam has a word for the idea underneath it: amanah. A trust -- something valuable, placed temporarily into your hands, carrying obligations precisely because it does not ultimately belong to you. One of the Qur'an's central instructions concerning authority is remarkably direct: " Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice." (Qur'an 4:58) Notice the language: between people. Not between Muslims. The obligation is not sectarian. And amanah isn't merely generosity with other people's money you've been entrusted with. It is responsible stewardship of it. That's why the boring procurement story may actually be one of my favorite examples. Finding a way to save New York's schools more than $100 million by fixing a procurement system "built for 2006" doesn't make for soaring political theater. But being compassionate while carelessly wasting what you've been entrusted with isn't amanah. Taking responsibility for the machinery of government -- including the boring parts -- is. | | ---|---|--- 'Adl : Justice, Even When It Costs Your Side There is another pattern in Mamdani's politics: his own community's claim to belonging has never required somebody else's exclusion. He has spoken unapologetically about Muslims belonging in the halls of power while making an equally explicit commitment to protecting Jewish New Yorkers from antisemitism. His political vocabulary continually widens the circle -- immigrants, Black women, trans New Yorkers, single mothers, workers, tenants, people who voted against him. Islam has a word for the principle underneath that: ' adl, justice. And the Qur'anic standard for it is considerably more demanding than "be fair to your friends." " Stand firmly for justice, as witnesses for God, even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or your close relatives." (Qur'an 4:135) Another passage goes further: " Do not let the hatred of a people lead you away from justice. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness." (Qur'an 5:8) Put those together and you get something quite different from identity politics in its crudest form. Islam does not say: acquire power so your people finally get their turn. It says that acquiring power increases your obligation to justice -- including toward people who are not yours, people you dislike, and people whose interests may conflict with your own. Power is supposed to expand the moral circle, not shrink it. Rahmah : The Humanity of Both the Prisoner and the Guard Then there is Rikers Island. During Ramadan, Mamdani became the first New York City mayor to break the fast there. He prayed and ate alongside incarcerated Muslims, many of them still awaiting trial, and Muslim corrections officers. Think about the political symbolism available to him in that room: prisoners on one side, guards on the other, the state and the people confined by the state, breaking bread together, along with their mayor. Asked why he went, Mamdani didn't reach for a criminal-justice talking point. "This is me just being a Muslim New Yorker," he said. "There are some for whom that is a political act." A sitting United States senator responded by posting a photograph of Mamdani's Rikers iftar next to an image of the burning Twin Towers. Mamdani kept going -- seventeen public iftars that Ramadan, from City Hall to a mosque in Jamaica, Queens. Islam has a word for the instinct underneath this, too: rahmah , mercy -- not mercy in the weak sense of refusing judgment or pretending harm doesn't matter, but mercy as a governing disposition. It's the refusal to let an institution, an offense, a uniform, a political category, or somebody's usefulness to you exhaust your understanding of their humanity. The prisoner is human. The guard is human. The mayor's obligation to recognize that does not disappear because recognizing both at once makes for messier politics. Human dignity comes before the label the state has stamped on you. Caring for the People who've been Made Powerless There is another Arabic word worth knowing: mustad 'afin. It appears repeatedly in the Qur'an, and it means something close to those who have been made weak -- people rendered vulnerable or powerless by the conditions around them. Poverty, vulnerability and marginalization are not always simply characteristics people happen to possess. Sometimes people have been made powerless by systems built by people with considerably more power. Mamdani's politics is unusually concrete about who government exists to notice. Not "working families" or "the middle class" as political abstractions, but the halal food-cart vendor, the construction worker, the tenant, the aging grandmother, the single mother trying to get a child to school and still make it to work on time. His administration's first citywide Racial Equity Plan makes some of that attention measurable: goals across housing, maternal mortality, education, employment and transportation, accompanied by an explicit invitation to New Yorkers to hold the administration accountable for meeting them. That is amanah again, in another key -- your attention, from a position of power, deliberately flowing toward people with the least power to reward you for giving it. Tell the Truth. Especially to Power. There is another dimension of Islamic leadership worth addressing, because mercy without moral courage can become mere politeness. Islam does not only tell people to recognize injustice. It places an obligation on them to confront it. The Prophet Muhammad put it with startling directness: " Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart -- and that is the weakest of faith." (Sahih Muslim 49) Look at the hierarchy. If you possess the power to stop something wrong, use it. If you don't, speak against it. And if even speaking is beyond your capacity, at minimum do not let power persuade your conscience that wrong has become right. That sheds some light on another feature of Mamdani's political style: he can be remarkably unwilling to euphemize. He has said publicly that Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, describing him as the architect of a genocide against Palestinians and pointing to the International Criminal Court's warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity. But the more revealing part is the principle Mamdani says he is applying. He has also called the atrocities of October 7 a horrific war crime, and asked about the apparent contradiction, his answer was essentially that there isn't one: humanity is universal. "We cannot pick and choose which crimes against humanity we oppose," he said. ICC warrants should be treated consistently, whether they concern Netanyahu, Yahya Sinwar, Vladimir Putin, or anyone else. That is almost a case study in Qur'an 5:8 -- do not let your hatred of one people cause you to abandon justice, or for that matter, your allegiance to another. Mamdani has also been careful about the distinction between moral condemnation and lawful authority, insisting that he can say what he believes to be true about Netanyahu while acknowledging the legal limits on what a New York mayor can actually do. Say what you believe to be true. Do what is actually within your authority. Don't pretend to possess powers you don't. And don't pretend not to see wrongdoing simply because the person responsible is powerful. That is a recognizable Islamic moral posture. But the harder test came much closer to home: his own office. For twenty-five years, New Yorkers exposed to the toxic dust of September 11 fought to understand what their government knew about the air they were breathing. In September, Mamdani's administration settled two longstanding lawsuits over those records and released an initial cache of more than 170,000 pages, including records survivors, first responders and advocates had sought for years. And the mayor did not sanitize what they contained. "These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it and how they acted to limit liability," he said. They include records of asbestos appearing throughout environmental testing and discussions within the Giuliani administration about health hazards and potential liability. Mamdani's administration committed $34 million to a public portal where the records can be examined freely, with substantially more documents scheduled for release. Why does that belong in an essay about Islamic leadership? Because the public's trust is also an amanah , and truth is part of what has been entrusted. Islam is exceptionally severe about rulers who deceive the people they govern. In a hadith recorded in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the Prophet warns that a ruler whom God entrusts with people and who dies while deceiving them faces an extraordinary condemnation: Paradise is forbidden to him. That is not treated as a minor lapse of political ethics. It is a fundamental betrayal of the trust itself. Look, then, at the choice facing the new administration. It possessed information damaging to the institution it now controlled. That institution had spent years resisting disclosure. The people had a right to know. Mamdani, the first among those who've held that office, gave the truth back to them -- almost a literal enactment of amanah : restore what has been entrusted to you to those to whom it belongs. That connects two episodes that otherwise look completely different. Calling Netanyahu a war criminal means speaking clearly about someone extraordinarily powerful. Releasing the 9/11 records means exposing wrongdoing by the government Mamdani himself now leads. Different circumstances, same underlying proposition: power does not acquire a right to comfortable lies merely because exposing the truth is inconvenient. If you can change the wrong with your hand, change it. If you cannot, speak. And if you are entrusted with the truth itself, give it back. And Yes, Let's Talk About Sharia This is approximately where somebody on cable television starts shouting It 'S sHaRiA!!!!, which is revealing, because most Americans encountering that word in political rhetoric have never actually been told what it means. Shari'ah does not mean "Muslims take over the government and make everybody Muslim." The word originally evokes a path leading to water -- a way toward the source of life. In Islam, it came to mean the divinely guided path for how a person should live. It refers broadly to the Islamic path of moral and religious life -- encompassing worship, fasting, charity, marriage, contracts, inheritance, treatment of neighbors, obligations toward the poor, personal conduct, and, yes, traditions of jurisprudence and governance, when the societal situation supports them. Is Zohran Mamdani trying to make New Yorkers live under Islamic religious law? No. There is no evidence he has ever proposed anything resembling that. The First Amendment and the U.S. Constitution he's sworn to uphold wouldn't permit it anyway. But there is an even more interesting answer: Islam itself wouldn 't permit what his critics are imagining, either. The Qur'an says it with startling economy: " There is no compulsion in religion." (Qur'an 2:256) That wasn't invented by twenty-first-century Muslims trying to make Islam sound palatable to liberal Americans. Classical Qur'anic commentators have understood the verse as a prohibition against forcing people to become Muslim for well more than a millennium. The Qur'an elsewhere asks Muhammad himself: if God had willed, everyone could have believed -- given that, " Would you then compel people to become believers?" (Qur'an 10:99), asking directly whether Muhammad would seek to override God's own wisdom and purpose in creating different communities of faith. Of course not. And the Qur'an does something even more interesting when discussing Jews and Christians. In chapter 5, it asks why Jews are bringing disputes to Muhammad when they already have the Torah, containing God's judgment. It tells the Christians, people of the Gospel, to judge according to what God revealed to them in it. And then it says: " For each of you We have appointed a law and a way. Had God willed, He could have made you one community... so compete with one another in good works." (Qur'an 5:48) The Qur'an itself recognizes religious communities living alongside one another without requiring that their religious laws become identical. That principle became something recognizable throughout Islamic history: legal pluralism. Muslim governments were certainly not modern liberal democracies, and the historical record contains hierarchies, restrictions, injustices and episodes of persecution that shouldn't be airbrushed away. But Jewish and Christian communities commonly retained their own religious institutions and jurisdiction over significant areas of communal and family life, alongside the Muslim courts and public order. This isn't a modern reinterpretation invented because pluralism became fashionable. It has roots at the beginning. Most Americans, myself included, were never taught any of this. An entire civilization -- centuries of a way of life across huge portions of the planet, giving rise to astonishing developments in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, technology, and philosophy that seeded the European Renaissance -- completely erased from our textbooks. (What a deprivation of humanity's moral and intellectual inheritance.) For our purposes here, three moments in Islamic history are worth knowing. Medina: One City, More Than One Faith When Muhammad became the political leader of Medina, he did not require its Jewish communities to become Muslim. The document traditionally known as the Constitution or Charter of Medina established agreements among the city's different communities concerning mutual defense, obligations, security and dispute resolution while explicitly recognizing religious distinction. The exact constitutional meaning of that document is debated by historians, and we shouldn't pretend seventh-century Medina was a modern liberal republic. It wasn't. But the underlying fact is difficult to miss: Muhammad, the founder of Islam, governed a city containing communities that did not share his religion, and their continued religious existence was recognized rather than erased. The Qur'an's own language about Jews judging by Torah and Christians by Gospel belongs to that same world. Islam did not require everyone living under Muslim political authority to become Muslim. Jerusalem: What Conquest Could Have Looked Like -- and Didn't Then consider Jerusalem. When the Muslim armies took the city in 638, Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab came personally to receive its surrender. This was a conquest -- we don't need to sanitize that word. What matters is what happened next. The Christian population was not massacred. Their churches were not systematically destroyed. Their holy places remained Christian places of worship; indeed, the protection Umar granted Jerusalem's Christians and their churches would be invoked by later Muslim authorities as a reason Christians' sacred spaces could not simply be confiscated. And something else happened. Under Byzantine Christian rule, Jews had been barred from Jerusalem. After the Muslim conquest, Jewish life returned to the city. Jewish historical sources themselves remember Umar as permitting Jews to reestablish a presence in Jerusalem after centuries of exclusion. That comparison becomes especially uncomfortable when we move forward several centuries. When Christian Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, the conquest culminated in the mass killing of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Contemporary accounts differ wildly about the number killed, but not about the reality of the slaughter. Al-Andalus: Not Utopia. Something More Interesting. And then there is Muslim Spain. Al-Andalus gets romanticized sometimes as an interfaith paradise where Muslims, Christians and Jews all held hands and invented algebra together. History is messier than that -- there were legal inequalities, conflicts, periods of persecution, rulers considerably better than others. But something extraordinary nevertheless happened there. For centuries, Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in the same civilization and participated in overlapping intellectual, commercial, medical, diplomatic and cultural worlds. Jewish intellectual life flourished spectacularly during important periods of Muslim rule. Christians continued living and worshiping there. Arabic became a language of scholarship crossing religious boundaries. And non-Muslims didn't merely survive at the margins -- some rose astonishingly high. Hasdai ibn Shaprut, a Jewish physician and scholar in tenth-century Cordoba, became one of Caliph Abd al-Rahman III's most important diplomats and officials, directing customs administration and conducting diplomatic negotiations with Christian kingdoms on the caliph's behalf. A century later, Samuel ha-Nagid -- Jewish poet, Talmudic scholar and statesman -- became vizier of Granada and commanded Muslim armies. Pause on that one: a Jewish religious scholar became one of the most powerful officials in a Muslim kingdom and commanded its Muslim soldiers. That does not prove medieval Islam secretly invented twenty-first-century egalitarian democracy. It proves something much simpler and harder to square with the cartoon version of Islamic civilization Americans are routinely sold: religious difference and Muslim political leadership were not inherently incompatible with civic collaboration, intellectual exchange, communal autonomy, or even extraordinary positions of public trust. There is a historical lineage here -- Medina, Jerusalem, Cordoba and Granada. Different centuries, different political systems, imperfect human beings producing imperfect societies. But the underlying idea keeps appearing: Muslim leadership does not require everybody being led to become Muslim. Which brings us back to New York. His Muslimness Doesn't Need an Apology For decades, prominent American Muslims in public life have often been pushed toward one of two performances: minimize the faith until everyone is reassured that you're harmless, or allow your Muslim identity to become the entire political story. Mamdani does neither. He fasts while running America's largest city. He says Assalamu alaikum in public. He visits mosques. He was sworn in at midnight on his grandfather's Qur'an and ceremonially on a centuries-old Qur'an from the Schomburg collection that once belonged to the Black Puerto Rican historian Arturo Schomburg. And then he goes back to talking about buses and child care and housing and garbage and procurement reform. That is genuine normalization. His faith neither disappears nor demands dominion. It is simply there, forming the person exercising power. And perhaps that's why the anti-Sharia hysteria is so revealing. Christians are allowed to enter public life shaped by "love thy neighbor." Jews are allowed to arrive carrying centuries of Jewish ethical thought. Secular humanists are allowed to possess deeply held convictions about dignity, equality and human flourishing. Of course a Muslim public official is shaped by Islam. Why wouldn 't he be? The relevant constitutional question isn't whether his faith influences his moral character. It is whether he uses government to impose that faith on everyone else. Mamdani doesn't. And the irony is that the religious tradition his haters panic over, actually contains explicit instructions against religious compulsion and a long history of governing communities in which multiple religions continued to exist. A Muslim does not become threatening because he arrives in public life carrying a moral tradition. The question is what that tradition teaches him to do with power, and how faithfully he exercises it. The Hardest Test Yet Which brings us to September 11. A Muslim mayor of New York presiding over the twenty-fifth anniversary of the attacks is about as symbolically loaded a situation as American public life can produce. Some critics -- including a former mayor of the city -- argued openly that Mamdani's faith itself made his presence at the memorial inappropriate. Think about what that claim actually does: it collapses "Muslim" back into "the men who did this," as if nearly two million Muslim Americans haven't spent the intervening quarter-century living, working, raising families, serving in uniform, becoming doctors and teachers and firefighters and public servants, and burying their own dead in this country. Mamdani had every moral right to be furious. But his response was not to center his own injury. He went to firehouses and stood with the FDNY as it remembered the members it lost. He stood with police officers and their families, and joined an interfaith memorial service at St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church. And when he spoke about September 11, he spoke about New Yorkers. He told the story of an older man falling as the dust cloud raced toward him, and the people fleeing alongside him stopping, turning around, putting their arms beneath him, and lifting him back onto his feet. He spoke about the flotilla of boats that converged on Lower Manhattan after the Coast Guard called for help -- people carrying strangers, people helping children and elderly New Yorkers aboard, a city refusing to leave people behind. Those who attacked New York, Mamdani said, believed they could break the city at its fractures. They were wrong. That is an extraordinary thing for America's first Muslim mayor to say at the twenty-fifth anniversary of an attack that transformed Muslim life in this country -- not because he apologized for being Muslim, which he didn't, and not because he demanded that the day acknowledge what happened to Muslims afterward, which he didn't need to. He simply fulfilled the responsibility of the office he holds: these people suffered, this is my city, I am their mayor, I will remember with them. New Yorkers noticed the difference in his performance and character. A Suffolk University poll released that same week found him with strong approval numbers and a majority saying he'd exceeded their expectations in office, with nearly three-quarters of voters saying he should attend the commemoration despite demands that he stay away. Before reading this essay, perhaps you would simply have called his response grace. Now you know another word for what you're seeing: amanah. His critics looked at a Muslim standing at Ground Zero and concluded that Islam was the problem. Look again. Islam may be part of the reason he understood how profound his obligation was to be there. Let's Not Canonize Him There is an important caution here. Eight months is not a mayoral term. Mamdani is a politician, not a saint, and Islam itself gives us particularly good reasons to resist confusing those categories. Leadership is tested across the whole stewardship, especially once stewardship becomes inconvenient -- when allies want favors, when budgets force painful tradeoffs, when a mistake needs admitting and admitting it is politically expensive, when somebody you despise deserves justice, when popularity and principle stop pointing in the same direction. New York will test Mamdani on all of that. It should. But the pattern so far is not nothing. Amanah : power as trust. ' Adl: justice beyond tribe. Rahmah : mercy as a way of encountering other human beings. Concern for the mustad 'afin: attention to those power has rendered powerless. The duty to confront wrongdoing : act where you have power, speak where you do not, and refuse inwardly to call evil good. And no compulsion in religion : faith expressed through character rather than forced through the state. And there is one more thing, which isn't a category of jurisprudence but may matter almost as much: he smiles. He jokes about chai and biryani and the outrageous price of New York coffee. He has talked about his grandmother teaching him that following the Prophet's example included smiling at people. There is something genuinely attractive about an Islam presented to America not primarily as prohibition, grievance, apologetics or theological argument, but simply lived: feed people, know your neighbors, protect the vulnerable, keep your promises, don't waste what you've been entrusted with, stand for justice even when it costs your own side, tell the truth when power would rather you didn't, recognize the humanity of the prisoner and the guard, protect people whose religion is different from yours, show up when your neighbors mourn, and smile at people. Maybe the most useful thing Mamdani is doing for Americans' understanding of Islam isn't explaining Islam at all. He's just practicing it where everyone can see him. None of this requires New York to become Muslim. It requires a Muslim entrusted with New York to take seriously what his religion asks of him. And perhaps, after twenty-five years in which Americans have been trained to hear Arabic words and imagine danger, there is something quietly corrective about learning a few different ones. Amanah. 'Adl. Rahmah. Trust. Justice. Mercy. You already knew what they looked like. Now you know some of their names. * Melissa Chaudhry is a two-time candidate for Congress and the wife of disabled American veteran Muhammad Zahid Chaudhry, who was illegally abducted and detained by ICE for four months. body:
Hi Peter, We asked. You answered. Vermont is expected to receive approximately $92.7 million from a settlement holding Meta and Big Tech accountable. That’s a significant investment in our state, and I wanted to hear directly from you about how you think those funds should be used. So we asked: **How should Vermont invest these incoming funds from the Meta settlement?** Over 50 Vermonters from across the state took the time to share their ideas on where the money should be invested here in Vermont. Here’s what you told us: **28%** — Mental health resources for young Vermonters
**22%** — Universal primary care
**21%** — Property tax relief
**15%** — Affordable housing
**6%** — School construction and infrastructure
**2%** — Afterschool programs And Vermonters brought even more ideas to the table. Some called for stronger investments in children and schools. Others suggested playgrounds, community centers and libraries, media literacy, student loan relief, and even creating a sovereign wealth fund. One Vermonter in Shaftsbury reminded us that before investing in new programs, the state should make sure we are being responsible with the programs we already have. Another Vermonter in Orwell suggested investing in Vermont’s farmers, especially as extreme weather and food insecurity continue to threaten our rural communities. **This is exactly what this campaign is about.** I don’t believe one candidate or one officeholder has all the answers. The challenges facing Vermont – from the cost of housing and health care to property taxes, child care, rural communities and our changing economy – are too critical for that. We need Vermonters at the table. And when I am Lieutenant Governor,**I will always make sure Vermonters have a seat at that table.** I’ll listen to your ideas, bring people together, and make sure the voices of working families, young people, seniors, farmers, small businesses and communities across our state are part of the decisions that shape our future. Over 50 Vermonters from across the state took the time to share their ideas on where the money should be invested here in Vermont. Some called for stronger investments in children and schools. Others suggested playgrounds, community centers and libraries, media literacy, student loan relief, and even creating a sovereign wealth fund. One Vermonter in Shaftsbury reminded us that before investing in new programs, the state should make sure we are being responsible with the programs we already have. Another Vermonter in Orwell suggested investing in Vermont’s farmers, especially as extreme weather and food insecurity continue to threaten our rural communities. subject: Did you catch Z’s email?
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Swing Left, [swingleft
body:
We’re aiming to knock 5,000 doors across 70 canvasses next weekend.
#
Hi there,
Did you catch Z’s email from last week?
**This upcoming weekend, Saturday, September 19th and Sunday, September 20th, is our third Weekend of Action, and our biggest yet! Together, the Swing Left community is aiming to knock 5,000 doors across more than 70 canvasses—and if you live near a target swing district or state, the best way to make an immediate impact on the midterm elections is to join us.**
[**RSVP for our Weekend of Action Kickoff Training at noon ET on Saturday, September 19th, where the Swing Left team will provide you with training on how to have deep conversations at the doors with Ground Truth, help you feel confident and comfortable, and assign you a set of doors in a nearby swing district or state.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2361?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=1&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)
**[RSVP For Canvass Training](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2361?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=2&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)**
Ground Truth is Swing Left’s innovative deep canvassing program where volunteers are having substantive conversations with voters—Independents, waning Democrats, and squishy Republicans—about the direction of the country and their likelihood to vote for Democrats.
Through these conversations, volunteers are finding persuadable voters and learning more about what voters want from their candidates. The insights gathered are made available to campaigns and party committees so they can refine their messaging, targeting, and outreach to build winning campaigns.
With fewer than 50 days until Election Day, every Ground Truth conversation with a voter is critical to helping Democrats flip the House and Senate. [**RSVP to join Swing Left volunteers across the country this weekend in a swing district near you.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2361?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=3&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)
Thank you,
The Team at Swing Left
\-------- Forwarded message --------
From: Z at Swing Left
Subject: Can you join us next weekend?
Hi there,
Z here, Voter Contact Director at Swing Left! I’m reaching out about our upcoming Weekend of Action on September 19th and 20th.
**We’re aiming to knock 5,000 doors across 70 canvasses, and we still need more canvass hosts and volunteers to help us make it happen.**
In total, we’re working to have hundreds of thousands of conversations with voters by Election Day—and it’s going to take all of us doing what we can to reach that goal.
**If you’d like to be a part of our upcoming Weekend of Action, there are two different ways to take action today:**
1. [**You can host a canvass to talk with voters in the swing districts and states we need to win this November.
**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2361?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=4&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)

1. [**Or, you can sign up to join us Saturday for a canvass training, get the tools you need, and be assigned a set of doors to knock in a Swing Left target race during the Weekend of Action.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2362?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=5&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)

With just over 7 weeks until Election Day, every conversation each of us has on the doors will help build the relationships and organizing power Democrats need to flip the House and Senate. So please join us in whatever way works best for you!
Hope to see you out there,
Z Mooney
Voter Contact Director, Swing Left
P.S. Don’t live near a swing district or state? [**You can make calls from the comfort of your home to connect with voters in high-stakes swing districts nationwide.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/499?utm_source=em20260915-2789&t=6&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)

**Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power.** Right now, Swing Left is investing in grassroots organizing in key swing districts and initiatives across the country to flip the House and win the Senate and critical states in 2026. [**If you’d like to help support our work, you can make a donation using this link.**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_sl_footer?refcode=em20260915-1&t=7&refcode2=2789_1562180_4jERDA&akid=2789%2E1562180%2E4jERDA)

name: Matthew Davis, LCV
subject: TAKE ACTION: Protect clean air in your community!
body:
To view this mail in a browser, copy https://links.messages.lcv.org/servlet/MailView?ms=MTM5NTUzMDkS1&r=NjA3MDU0MTAzNTc3S0&j=MjU0MDQ0NzE1MwS2&mt=1&rt=0 into your browser.
Tell Congress: Stand Up for Clean Air!

Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is scheming with Congressional
Republicans to erase decades of progress on cleaner air and vehicle standards,
putting communities and the Clean Air Act at risk, all for their fossil fuel
cronies. This would put millions of peopleaffected by air pollution at even greater risk, while increasing transportation
costs and lining the pockets of Big Oil.

Rolling back these safeguards is both dangerous and costly — people already have
to pay more money for fuel, and this will limit their options to seek cheaper,
more fuel efficient vehicles and electric engines.

Join LCV in taking action today to protect clean air and families’ budgets, and
stop this misuse of congressional procedures and the Congressional Review Act
for more handouts to Big Oil.

Tell your member of Congress: Vote NO on clean air rollbacks! https://links.messages.lcv. ADD YOUR NAME https://links.messages.lcv. Peter, American families deserve clean, safe air to breathe. But right now, Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is scheming with
Congressional Republicans to erase decades of progress on cleaner air and vehicle standards. This would put millions of peopleaffected by air pollution at even greater risk, while increasing transportation
costs and lining the pockets of Big Oil. Tell your member of Congress: VOTE NO on clean air attacks >> https://links.messages.lcv. TAKE ACTION NOW https://links.messages.lcv.org/els/v2/k_ypT7- Blocking pollution limits for vehicles is both dangerous and costly — people
already have to pay more for fuel, and this will limit their options to seek
cheaper, more fuel efficient vehicles and electric engines. Instead of providing
families with some relief, this is yet another handout to Trump’s Big Oil
buddies. Our communities need more clean air protections and more relief from skyrocketing bills — not more rollbacks and gas price hikes.Cleaner efficient vehicles that go further on a gallon of gas, electric vehicles
and expanded charging options, maritime vessels that run on electricity, and
more accessible public transit are all great affordability solutions that also
deliver cleaner air, and we need more of those kinds of solutions. Protect our air and affordability! Add your name today >> https://links.messages.lcv. Thank you for joining LCV in the fight for the affordable, cleaner climate
future we all need and deserve. Matthew Davis

_Nadia was only 15 years old when they went looking for her. _ A pastor had called House Parent Project, a children's home in Mexico. He knew Nadia was in danger. He even knew the Metro station in Mexico City where she could often be found.So the house parents went and they found her. But to understand what happened next, you need to know where Nadia came from. She never knew her father. Her mother lived an unstable and dangerous life, moving from one man to another. Nadia was the oldest of three little girls. Her youngest sister was given up for adoption. But Nadia grew up with almost nothing and no one. She survived on the streets of Mexico City, surrounded by drugs, prostitution, abandonment, and exploitation. Imagine being 15 years old and wondering if there is a single adult in this world you can trust. That was the girl they found near that Metro station. There was doubt in Nadia's eyes. But they asked her to give them a chance.

They told her something every child deserves to hear: **You are loved. **They promised to protect her and help her get an education. And Nadia willingly went with them. She left behind a horrible life and came home to parents who would raise her as their own. body:
A gut check on gas prices, why I'm optimistic about November, and what's coming next
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139277892/646818983/-1038038363?refcode=ITT_ATA_EM_NF_BeshearBriefing_260915_T1_1&utm_campaign=itt_ata_em_nf_beshearbriefing_260915_t1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTAzNjMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYTQ1ZGJjMzItNTliMS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5ZjFkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=KqCv8CAvyjsT7mOLCP1XtZRVJy21xHU96hA1hpyoa5E=&emci=c47f869c-27b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=a45dbc32-59b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=17458827)
Peter,

I wanted to start something new — a semi-regular note, straight from me. Here we go:

Let's start with something I know is hitting your wallet hard: gas and diesel prices just hit record highs. Diesel costs are the highest they’ve ever been, full stop. That's not just a huge blow for our farmers. It increases the price of moving groceries, building materials, and just about everything else you buy.

Why is this happening? The war in Iran that Donald Trump started is cutting off oil supply and driving up prices at the pump. Add on his tariffs, and you've got working families getting squeezed from every direction: higher costs to fill up the car, higher costs to fill the fridge, higher costs just to get through the week.

Here's the thing, though — I think this is a turning point. Families are feeling the impact of this administration, and they want new leaders who will deliver real results.

I've traveled to a lot of places this year that don't always vote for Democrats, and I'll tell you — I'm optimistic. I think we're going to win big this November, and I think some of those wins are going to come from places nobody expects.

That's why I'm spending the next two months on the road, doing everything I can to help good candidates get across the finish line, in red states, purple states, and everywhere in between. Democrats can win anywhere, and we ought to be showing up everywhere.

One more thing before I let you go, my new book, _**[Go and Do Likewise](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139277894/646818985/-1106739200?refcode=ITT_ATA_EM_NF_BeshearBriefing_260915_T1_1&utm_campaign=itt_ata_em_nf_beshearbriefing_260915_t1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTAzNjMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYTQ1ZGJjMzItNTliMS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5ZjFkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=KqCv8CAvyjsT7mOLCP1XtZRVJy21xHU96hA1hpyoa5E=&emci=c47f869c-27b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=a45dbc32-59b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=17458827)**_ , comes out next week. It's about reclaiming faith as a force for good, and it's the most personal thing I've ever put my name on. I hope it's a conversation starter, whatever your faith looks like. I also hope that if you live near any of the stops on _**[my book tour](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139277895/646818988/-674273269?refcode=ITT_ATA_EM_NF_BeshearBriefing_260915_T1_1&utm_campaign=itt_ata_em_nf_beshearbriefing_260915_t1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTAzNjMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYTQ1ZGJjMzItNTliMS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5ZjFkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=KqCv8CAvyjsT7mOLCP1XtZRVJy21xHU96hA1hpyoa5E=&emci=c47f869c-27b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=a45dbc32-59b1-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=17458827)**_ , you’ll come say hi.

Now here's my ask — and it's not for money. Just hit reply and tell me: how are rising costs hitting your family right now? How are you feeling about the election this November? Are you knocking doors, phone banking, or helping a candidate in some other way this year? Or honestly, whatever's on your mind — let me know!

Talk soon,
Andy | | **Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and In This Together PAC are working to support leaders who will lead with compassion and decency, reject anger politics, and always do what's right. Will you donate today to support In This Together's mission?** [DONATE](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139277896/646818989/753972181?refcode=ITT_ATA_EM_NF_BeshearBriefing_260915_T1_1&utm_campaign=itt_ata_em_nf_beshearbriefing_260915_t1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjEvMS8xMTAzNjMiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYTQ1ZGJjMzItNTliMS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5ZjFkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=KqCv8CAvyjsT7mOLCP1XtZRVJy21xHU96hA1hpyoa5E=)
